Capabilities beyond upstream are wz features, composed by Kconfig and SCE like any other

Owner 2026-10-30 supersedes the caveat above: wz is a framework, upstream is one preset

11.intent: Multi-layer testing strategy: byte-equivalence parity, wire replay, upstream interop, no-alloc guard, drift detection, fuzz.

11/11.1.intent: Cross-backend parity gate — every algorithm/codec with sce:test-vector runs on both backends and is byte-diffed; gate on merge.

11/11.2.intent: Wire replay tests — pcap captures from upstream zenoh peers replayed into generated stack with declared expected event sequence.

11/11.3.intent: Upstream interop CI — dockerized zenohd + AP node + MCU host-mode build (lwIP shim, renode/QEMU later) asserting full handshake + pub/sub roundtrip.

11/11.4.intent: MCU heap prohibition enforced as five layers — direct trap, linker wrap, libc pin, call-graph reachability, exception ban — not runtime trap alone.
rationale_bullets: Layer 1 direct trap: malloc/calloc/realloc/free stubs emit __builtin_trap on call.
Layer 2 linker --wrap: -Wl,--wrap on alloc symbols routes libc-internal indirect calls to traps.
Layer 3 libc pin: newlib-nano or picolibc tiny stdio prevents allocating printf path.
Layer 4 call-graph: post-link analyzer rejects any reach from out/mcu to deny-listed allocator.
Layer 5 exception ban: -fno-exceptions/-fno-rtti/-fno-unwind-tables blocks libstdc++ machinery.

11/11.5.intent: Drift gate: every emitted file carries source-hash + template-hash; sce-build verify recomputes and fails on mismatch; manual edits to out/ forbidden.
rationale_bullets: Per-file header carries source-hash + template-hash (sha256 over inputs and sce-build binary).
sce-build verify recomputes both hashes and fails the gate on mismatch (CI + pre-commit).
Fixed artifact set: out/{ap,mcu}, Cargo.toml, CMakeLists.txt, linker fragments, sce_sourcemap.json.
Manual edits to out/ forbidden: path is RFC or sce:extern; exceptions tracked with expiry date.
sce_sourcemap.json hash mismatch surfaces as traceability/sourcemap-source-hash-mismatch.

11/11.6.intent: Adversarial input fuzz testing on generated codec/parsers; deferred Phase D+ work; complements §11.1 cross-backend parity.

2/2.3.intent: MCU-class permanent constraints (no router, no aggregation, no heap, no scripting, no unbounded KeyExpr, no dynamic loading); AP unaffected.

2/2.4.intent: Six extensibility invariants: static-first, link-extensible, kinds-additive, library-not-monolith, platform gating, out/ SSoT.
rationale_bullets: Static-first, dynamic-opt-in: every MCU-static feature should admit an AP-dynamic variant.
Link drivers extensible: open set via target plugin, not closed enum.
Kinds additive: ForgeKind set grows; existing kinds remain stable across versions.
Generated code exports as library, not monolith: out/ap and out/mcu are library targets.
Platform gating only when physically necessary; keep pool/link/worker kinds platform-neutral.
out/ is SSoT-downstream: manual edits forbidden; new features land via SCE extensions.

3.intent: Four design invariants: zero-runtime abstraction, location transparency, strict SSoT, hardware-aware codegen.

3/3.1.intent: Zero-Runtime Abstraction — no vtables, no dynamic dispatch in the hot path; all bindings resolve at build time to direct calls (SCE AOT philosophy carried through).

3/3.2.intent: Location Transparency — SCXML uses logical identities; physical transport realization and addressing live in deploy.yaml; same SCXML deploys to AP or MCU.

3/3.3.intent: Strict SSoT — wire format / algorithms / FSMs defined once in SCXML+Forge; AP and MCU are descendants; cross-backend drift is a generator bug, not expected.

3/3.4.intent: Hardware-Aware Codegen — MCU code integrates with target SoC capabilities (SRAM placement, DMA pairing, alignment) declared via deploy.yaml; AP/MCU share no memory.

4.intent: Mapping of SCE existing capabilities, RFC-requested extensions, and watching-zenoh authoring scope.

4/4.2.intent: SCE extensions requested via RFC — new kinds (algorithm/link/buffer-pool/worker/bounded-collection), codec DSL, fragment pattern, C11 backend, no_std statechart, sce:extern, deploy fields.

4/4.3.intent: Project authoring scope — SCXML statecharts, Forge codec/algorithm/bounded-collection/link/pool/worker sources, deploy.yaml variants, runtime crates, optional API shim.

7/7.1.intent: AP backend stack — generated code on top of sce_core + sce_link_runtime_tokio + Rust std/bytes/tokio; tokio::spawn workers, mpsc channels, BytesMut pools.

7/7.2.intent: MCU stack — generated code over sce_forge_runtime_c + sce_link_runtime_lwip; cooperative tick scheduler with WCET budget; static pools + DMA descriptors.

7/7.3.intent: Shared runtime crates/headers — sce_core (AP only), sce_forge_runtime (Rust+C variants), sce_link_runtime_{tokio,lwip}, sce_intrinsics_runtime (whitelisted).

8.intent: Wire format layering: scouting/transport/network/zenoh/extensions; FSM, codec, link layers.

8/8.1.intent: Wire format stack layer diagram — Application -> Session FSM -> Network FSM -> Codec -> Link -> OS/HAL; bottom-up data flow on RX, top-down on TX.

8/8.2.intent: Session FSM sketch — Init/Scouting/Opening/Established/Closing path authored as session_unicast/multicast.scxml; full model lives in docs/session-fsm.md.

8/8.3.intent: Codec layer — one SCXML file per message type using RFC §5.B extensions (flags/vle/present-if/len-prefix/TLV); test vectors drive cross-backend parity.

8/8.4.intent: Link layer — kind=link SCXML files (UDP unicast/multicast/TCP/Serial/WS) with framer + RX-pool + backpressure declared; driver and address bound via deploy.yaml.

9.intent: Zero-copy: TX always zero-copy; RX happy path zero-copy; oversized/fragment stage-copy; pool placement; platform-aware link.

9/9.1.intent: TX path zero-copy — Codec encodes directly into pool slot, link send-from-slot, DMA reads via prebuilt descriptor; pool slot in DMA-coherent SRAM.

9/9.2.intent: RX happy path zero-copy — DMA writes pre-programmed RX slot; codec parses in place; event emitted with slot borrow; slot returned to freelist.

9/9.3.intent: Stage-copy RX path for oversized/multi-DMA — one copy DMA-slot to stage; build-time fragmentation analysis; stage_copy_policy warn/error/forbid per machine.

9/9.4.intent: Pool placement across .dtcm/.sram1/.flash regions; per-pool placement declared in kind source; memory regions in deploy.yaml; linker fragment ties them.

9/9.5.intent: Platform-aware link substrate: 5-row matrix (MCU bare_metal, linux+epoll, linux+io_uring, QNX, etc) sharing pool FSM.

intrinsics-runtime--symbol-surface.intent: Defines sce_intrinsics_runtime symbol surface (C11/Rust variants) for atomics/fences/cache/IRQ/RNG/HMAC/HW-sem.
inputs_bullets: RFC sec 5.I sce:extern whitelist — atomics, fences, cache maintenance, IRQ control
RFC sec 5.J.2 — statechart no_std HAL trait shape (ticks/wake/irq-save)
RFC sec 5.K target_plugin extension — per-SoC HMAC + HW semaphores out of core whitelist
session-fsm sec 2.7 G-SFM-5 — HMAC + RNG primitive ownership question (OQ-W15)
reassembly-fsm sec 6 — cache maintenance pinning (sec 5.E pool FSM call sites)
ARCHITECTURE sec 9.5 5-row matrix — same symbol set, different bodies per row
outputs_bullets: Categorized symbol table marking core whitelist vs target plugin per category
sec 5.J.2 statechart no_std HAL trait mapped onto these symbols

intrinsics-runtime--symbol-surface/2-3-c.intent: Cache maintenance core whitelist on MCU, no-op on AP linux (kernel-coherent); emitted only on §5.E pool lifecycle FSM edges; direct <sce:call> rejected.

intrinsics-runtime--symbol-surface/2-4-i.intent: IRQ control core whitelist (optional) — irq_save/irq_restore; only emitted for workers with sce:critical-section (RFC §5.D, Phase C+); MVP deploys do not use these.

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/1-framing-o.intent: Reassembly FSM between codec (Fragment) and network FSMs; chain key=(peer_zid, reliability) — two buffers per peer per upstream wire shape.
inputs_bullets: Chain key (peer_zid 16B, reliability 1bit); no priority, no sn_base in key
Wire: Fragment {sn:u64 VLE, payload:ZSlice, more bit, reliability bit}
FRAGMENT_FIRST/DROP exts patch-1+; legacy patch-0 infers first via empty+consecutive SN
Fragment classification: First / Continue / Final / Drop / unmatched-continue dropped at Router

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/10-next-ste.intent: Reassembly FSM unblocks Phase A SCXML authoring of sources/network/reassembly.scxml; deploy.yaml reassembly_pool block fully named; OQ-W22 closed.

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/2-1-hierarc.intent: ReassemblyDispatcher = Router dispatcher + N slot-FSM instances (N=slot_count, build-const); one-active-per-key. N identical slots via instantiation (Engines in pool), not orthogonal regions.
inputs_bullets: Router: Rust dispatcher (registry pattern) — routing-over-tables, not a state machine
Router map: chain-key→slot-index (bounded-collection<SlotEntry,N>); per-peer quota check
Slot: reassembly-protocol statechart, instantiated per slot as SCE Engine<ReassemblySlotPolicy>
Slot four states; real orthogonality is per-slot: memory-lifecycle ∥ reassembly-protocol FSM
<parallel> reserved for fixed distinct concerns, not N-identical slots (= instantiation)
Upstream divergence: shared bounded pool decoupled from peer count (vs upstream inline 2×peers)
Parity invariant: slot_count ≥ 2 × peer_table.capacity reproduces upstream no-exhaustion
MCU slot_count=4, AP=32 (OQ-W8); over-commits trade strict parity for memory cost
caveats_bullets: R311ij realized engine-free: <sce:action> + native more-bit guard, needs_script_engine=false
R311ij SN-consecutive not native-guardable -> dispatcher pre-classifies chunk vs ooo
R311ij FSM cross-compiles thumbv7em no_std; buffer = wz-side BoundedVec per slot

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/2-2-slot-st.intent: Slot four-state FSM: Empty → Receiving → Complete / TimedOut / Aborted (three terminals funnel back to Empty via slot release).
inputs_bullets: Empty: slot free, awaiting allocation from Router
Receiving: chain in progress; consecutive Continue allowed
Complete: Final received with consecutive SN
TimedOut: reassembly_timeout_ms expired
Aborted: 7 reasons (OOO/Drop/duplicate-First/oldest-wins/codec-error/unmatched/peer-drop)
Slot release transitions buffer-pool slot cpu-mut/cpu-ref → free (lifecycle FSM funnel)

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/2-3-router-.intent: Router = dispatcher (registry): routes Fragment.* to the chain-key's slot FSM instance; enforces per-peer quota; refuses second First on an open key (duplicate-first abort); not an SCXML region.

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/2-4-transit.intent: Eight detailed transitions across Slot states: Empty→Receiving (First), Receiving→Receiving (Continue), Final→Complete, plus 5 abort variants and Terminal→Empty release funnel.
outputs_bullets: §2.4.1 Empty→Receiving: Fragment.First admitted by Router (key not-active, quota OK, slot OK)
§2.4.2 Receiving→Receiving: Fragment.Continue with consecutive SN appends payload
§2.4.3 Receiving→Complete: Fragment.Final consecutive SN, emit message-complete event
§2.4.4 Receiving→Aborted: out-of-order Continue (non-consecutive SN, strict in-order)
§2.4.6 Receiving→Aborted: oldest-wins eviction by Router under pool pressure
§2.4.7 Receiving→Aborted: codec error on payload decode (§2.4.7a peer-drop via DROP ext)
§2.4.8 Terminal→Empty: slot release funnel; lifecycle FSM cpu-mut→free

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/2-5-out-of-.intent: Strict in-order policy (OQ-W21 closed): non-consecutive Continue aborts the chain (option 2 ratified); upstream consecutive-SN parity preserved.

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/2-6-mapping.intent: Mapping prose four-state Slot FSM (Empty/Receiving/Complete/TimedOut/Aborted) to RFC §5.M three-state high-level sketch (Idle/Active/Done) with terminal split.

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/3-tx-fragme.intent: TX fragmentation sibling FSM — chunks outbound NetworkMessage exceeding link MTU into Fragment.{First, Continue, Final} with consecutive SN.

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/4-timer-quo.intent: Reassembly timer / per-peer quota / pool config from deploy.yaml — reassembly_timeout_ms, per_peer_quota, slot_count, slot_size live under buffer_pools.reassembly_pool.
caveats_bullets: R311ij timeout = dispatcher worker-tick deadline-sweep, not an FSM <send delay> (SCE no <cancel>)
R311ij slots reused; sweep targets only the live slot, not stale (cf. RFC 815 GC)

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/5-trust-cla.intent: Trust-class interaction — reassembly forbidden on untrusted/session_arming links; established_session sibling instance receives reassembly bindings (OQ-W22 close).

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/6-buffer-po.intent: Buffer-pool lifecycle FSM (§5.E) interaction — reassembly slot acquire = pool slot cpu-mut; terminal release = cpu-mut/cpu-ref → free.
caveats_bullets: R51-R52 RxFrame { bytes: Vec u8 } owned — pool-slot zero-copy not yet wired
Pool-slot Rx borrows carry: wz-runtime-tokio §4.1 io_uring fixed-buffer opt-in

reassembly-fsm--prose-sketch/7-1-reassem.intent: Build-time reassembly capacity check — max_fragments × per_peer_quota × peer_table.capacity sufficiency for slot_count; hard error if violated.

Round 4009.decision_summary: Step T1 of L6 (tls on the cooperative engine). The trust policy is a parameter of the one secure channel, not a second channel: Pinned (the zid of the peer's key, decision D1, unchanged and still what an unconfigured session does) and Chain (the peer's certificate chain verifies against given roots). The library is built without a clock, so it checks no certificate date; the caller states the time (or none, for a device without a clock) and a verify hook holds every certificate of the chain to it. A name is checked only when the caller states one, which is pico's default. A server asks for a client chain only when given roots (mutual TLS). Key and signature types stay P-256 and ECDSA over SHA-256 until T4 and T5 read what real pico and zenohd certificates use.
changes_bullets: crates/wz-tls-mbedtls: wz_tls.c/.h gain wz_tls_identity_from_pem, wz_tls_trust_from_pem and wz_tls_session_open_chain (verify mode, CA chain, date hook, per-session peer-certificate requirement); the crypto config gains the PEM and base64 readers; channel.rs gains Identity::from_pem, Trust and Session::open_chain; tests/chain_trust.rs adds 11 tests against rustls 0.23 and an rcgen authority; docs/capi-pico-on-coop-engine.md records T1.
verification_bullets: On pc2: cargo test -p wz-tls-mbedtls --features vendored: 2 + 11 + 3 passed, 0 failed. The refusals (wrong root, wrong name, expired, not yet valid, no client certificate under mutual TLS, unvouched client chain) each assert a Mbed TLS code, and the clockless case accepts the same expired certificate. Chain client arena peak 26,656 bytes, held at 32 KiB. clippy -D warnings clean for the crate with --all-targets; cargo fmt clean. The Zephyr images were read (Kconfig selects the key reader through the X.509 core), not built: the kit lane needs the board.

Round 4010.decision_summary: The connect-manager test that guards the manager against carrying the machines of its peers is corrected a second time. The bound is now that the store is larger than the manager, which is what the invariant needs: the machines are in the store, and a manager that carried them would exceed the store, which holds them and not the rest of what the manager holds. Round 4012.decision_summary: Step T2 of L6. The dial and the accept of the secure channel under both policies, as the stream link's StreamDial and StreamListen, so the stream link runs over either unchanged. A chain stream offers NO credential zid: a router's zid is its own, not its key's, so the session takes the zid the peer states and the chain was the proof; a pinned stream is unchanged. The name a stream dial has is the address, so verify_name matches it against the IP SAN. A mutual policy missing its identity or roots is Unsupported and never connects. The listener never blocks on the network: one inbound handshake runs at a time (the arena holds one inbound session), each accept advances it, and a handshake that outlasts the deploy's clock budget, fails, or comes from a non-TLS or untrusted peer is dropped without failing the listener. The coop crate gains StreamListen for Box<L>.

The table-sharing structures upstream does not have (snapshots, shards) are named as values of a second policy that enters with its code.

Round 4021.decision_summary: The 1.10.2 item (b) of O4 is taken: a multicast group honours transport/multicast/compression/enabled, which zenoh 1.10.1 never read. A compressing group carries every datagram as a batch, the one-byte BatchHeader in front and the payload lz4-compressed when that is smaller: the JOIN beacon, each frame and each fragment of a chain, framed to the batch less the header so no datagram passes the group's batch size. Multicast has no handshake to switch the wrap on, so members must state the same, and a build without transport_compression refuses the open of a node that joins a group with the key set. Item (a) is recorded as measured: the same wire, so wz is unchanged.

Round 4022.decision_summary:
The host half of the parity program has a measurement that can be graded where it had none: the no-drop rate of the pico ABI against zenoh-pico (`scripts/host-bench/`, mode `nodrop` of `scripts/pico-compare.sh`). The upstream throughput examples send as fast as they can, and their control (pico on both sides) read "no samples", so no cell of them could be graded. The new publisher OFFERS a stated rate (a slot of one millisecond at a time), the subscriber counts what it is delivered, and the search (RFC 2544) doubles the rate and bisects to 5 percent: a rate stands when no put failed, every message was counted, the puts took at most 102 percent of the trial and at least 98 percent of the offered messages were put. The same two sources are built against zenoh-pico and against `libwz_capi_pico`.

A trial is valid only when the pinned CPUs were used by nothing else (the busy time of those CPUs less the CPU time of the two processes, over the CPU seconds the trial had, at most 10 percent; interrupt time is left out because the packets of a loopback stream are the test's own cost). This is what separates the hosts: on pc2, shared with other sessions' builds (load 15 to 30), every trial was disturbed and the unfiltered search read values tens of times apart between two repetitions of one condition, so none of its figures is kept; on pc3, which the owner said may be used freely, the three repetitions of every condition agree within 5 percent.

Measured on pc3 (TCP loopback peer, median of three, msg/s), with the puts batched per slot, which is how the upstream example reaches pico's best rate: 8 B at least 5.12 M for wz against 4.48 M for pico, 64 B 4.48 M against 4.00 M, 1 KiB 160 k against 310 k. With the puts one by one pico makes one `sendto` per put and reads 360 k at every size, and wz reads at least 5.12 M, 4.48 M and 190 k. So the pico ABI is ahead of pico by 12 to 14 percent on small messages in pico's best configuration, and BEHIND by half at 1 KiB. The round trip of the same ABI reads a tie at 10 to 11 microseconds. The wz figure at 8 B is a lower bound (the search stops at its cap).

A red of two other sessions' commits is paid in this round: `resource_budget_gate.py --check` failed on main since `b4a5d05f0b` and `97fb40d2a2` committed the stack chains of the FreeRTOS demo images `frt` and `frt2` in the stack gate, because the resource table must have a row for every committed chain and a row is a chain with a kit reading beside it, which a QEMU image has none of. The table now has a key `not_measured_on_the_kit` (image to reason) which the gate holds both ways (a declared image must have a committed chain, must not also have a row, and must give a reason); `frt` and `frt2` are declared in it. No row was invented for them.

The 1 KiB cell is a loss and its mechanism is read, not guessed: with one `sendto` per put on both sides, wz adds about two `futex` calls per put (298,725 calls for 150,000 puts against pico's 14), and 84 percent of its `sendto` calls are made by the writer thread and not by the thread that put. The zero-copy lend path (`OutboundTx::commit_at`) wakes the writer for every frame (`frame_landed`); the writer is asleep between two frames 20 microseconds apart; the sender-side flush that exists for a lone message (`flush_inline`, with its quiet-time and stream tests) is reached from the batch hook and not from this path. Writing a lone lent frame from the sender's thread by the same tests is the lever, and it is not attempted yet.

Round 4031.decision_summary:
Round 41 named the lever for the 1 KiB host cell: write a lone or large frame from the thread that put it, by the tests `flush_inline` already has. That was tried and measured, and it is not the lever. A frame that lands alone, or is 512 bytes or more, was written by its sender whenever the writer's role was free (`OutboundTx::send`, `send_reserved` and the pooled commit path), with the writer-queue tests (632 in the crate) and both clippy feature sets passing.

On pc3 it changed nothing: 1 KiB reads 155 k batched and 190 k one by one against 160 k and 190 k before, and 8 B and 64 B are unchanged (4.8 M and 4.48 M batched, 4.96 M and 4.48 M one by one). Per thread (`strace -f`, 1 KiB at 150,000 a second), 3 of 158,857 `sendto` calls came from the putting thread and the writer still took one `futex` pair per frame. By reading `recv_wire_tagged_with`, the writer takes the role together with a frame and keeps it until that frame is written, so at 190 k frames a second the role is almost never free to a sender. A sender that waited for the role is not safe: the writer can be waiting on the socket for the runtime thread the sender may be running on.

The change is not kept; the commit was dropped before any push. What is kept is the reading, in docs/upstream-parity.md, and the correction of the lever: the loss sits in the one-writer pipeline, so a fix has to shorten what the writer holds or take the hop out of the queue.

No code changed in this round.

The writer-queue tests of wz-runtime-tokio passed (632) and clippy -D warnings passed with and without runtime-zero-copy; 123 static gates ran with rc 0 on the tree that had the change. The change was then dropped and this round's tree holds only the document.
Not run: any further transport change, the role-hold shortening, hosted lanes.

Open levers, untried: let the writer give the role up between taking a frame and writing it so that a sender can write behind it; or take the sender-to-writer hop out of the queue with a hand-off the writer spins on before it parks; either changes the transport of every tokio link and needs the writer-queue tests and a measurement that small messages lose nothing. Round 4038.decision_summary: The observation round 4023 carried unexplained, a stock zenohd's admin listing losing its multicast locator after a mismatched member's datagram, is zenohd's own behavior and not a defect of wz. Upstream 1.10.2 returns an error from the receive task of a multicast link when a datagram does not decode (the batch fails to read, or the message does not decode) and then deletes the transport, so one such datagram from any member takes the group down for that zenohd. wz's receiver drops the datagram and goes on, which is the sturdier behavior and the one to keep: a member that disagrees about the compression wrap cannot end the group for the others. A comment of the receive path that said upstream also only drops a batch it cannot read was wrong and is corrected; the witness explains why its second member starts only after the first is listed.

Round 4041.decision_summary: The open questions of the session lifecycle contract are ruled under the standing criterion (cost ignored, the most correct long-term, textbook, ultimate), D10 to D15 of the design note. A listen intent is the passive form of open on the same peer machine, as RFC 4271 section 8.1.2 has two start events; the collision of two dialling ends is the rule link_admission already holds (D10). The close-ingress atom stays one atom (D11). Authority is a function of the verified commander per verb, default deny, with a compiled-in commander list for an image that has no pipe, and the control channel's authority is possession of the pipe (D12). The Hello source on a fixed profile is the scouting capability's (D13). The Zephyr witness follows the image that binds the verbs (D14). An open for an unplaced peer enters the bounded table and reports no_locator (D15). The atom's reason is graded against what remains. The grade stays PARTIAL; nothing is implemented by this round.

Round 4042.decision_summary: A router told every face of a south region its peer hat serves (the peers of a group it is the gateway of) each subscriber and queryable that another region held, unasked, by a flood to the region's faces, by the face-up replay, and again by the answer to the face's interest: a peer that had asked for nothing registered a declaration for each, and one that asked registered it two or three times. Upstream's peer hat sends a face that is not north-bound a declaration of another hat only for an interest the face holds (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/peer/pubsub.rs` @ `fn maybe_propagate_subscriber`: the face is north-bound, or a remote interest of it matches), and does not repropagate subscribers to a new south-bound peer at all (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/peer/pubsub.rs` @ `New south-bound peer remote; not propagating subscribers`). The router now does the same. The interest of such a face, subscribers and queryables alike, is kept in the interest store as push-reachable under a new role (PeerHat); what self advertises into that region goes to the faces whose interest matches, each at most once, and is retracted by id from the faces that were told it; the answer to the interest seeds what was said so that the push that follows does not say it again; the face-up replay of subscribers and queryables is not made to such a face; and a declaration that a peer of the region made is not pushed to another face of the region (its peers learn it over their own links, as the answer already withheld). The region of a peer NODE is north of it and keeps the flood and the replay of R2388, which a zenoh-pico peer attached to a node that is not a router needs because it never asks; attached to a router it does ask (_z_add_interest writes an Interest when the session is a client, has a router peer, or is on a multicast transport), so nothing it relies on is withdrawn. The advertisement of a multicast group's subscribers goes through the same rule. Upstream's regions test, measured a process per test, goes from 64 to 78 of 126: scenario 6 putsub and getque, half of scenarios 3 and 7. The unit tests that watched a peer for the advertisements of a router now have the peer ask first; the two that tested the replay of R2388 and R2890 run on a peer node, and a new one holds that the peer of a router is told nothing until it asks.

Round 4047.decision_summary: Layer C0mut could not run on a build host, and the carry that called it a bx environment issue named the symptom and not the cause. The sweep starts its cargo child with `subprocess.run`, which closes every descriptor above 2, while the host's environment tells that child about a jobserver on descriptors 3 and 4 (MAKEFLAGS), so the child found nothing there; and the host puts sccache in front of rustc (RUSTC_WRAPPER) while the sweep builds incrementally on purpose (round 3140), which sccache refuses outright, so the baseline could not run `rustc -vV` and the sweep said the unmutated tree was not green. The sweep now builds its cargo child from `sweep_env`: no jobserver variables the child cannot reach, no compiler-cache wrapper it cannot use (a cache serves a crate compiled once from a clean tree, and this sweep recompiles one crate after a one-line edit a hundred times, which incremental state serves). Everything else of the caller's environment is kept. A selftest drives both directions: the variables are removed and nothing else is.

Round 4049.decision_summary: Decision D10 of the session lifecycle is built. A listen intent is the passive form of open on the same peer machine, as RFC 4271 section 8.1.2 has two start events: the machine gains Passive and PassiveUp, a passive peer is dialled by nobody, holds the session the peer opens, and goes back to waiting when it is lost, while a dialling open is the stronger and dials a passive peer as well. One tail reader gives the key open/passive/<peer-zid> to every profile, the control port says open passive, the status read says passive, and the contract table holds two passive cases judged on the mode the opener was asked in. On AP an accepted session whose key proved the zid is claimed by a waiting peer; on the fixed profile the manager is told the verified accepted sessions each tick.

Round 4054.decision_summary: O4 (h), the Timestamp ZID bound, was reported to the SCE session and answered: the decode of a bounded length-ref field is meant to refuse a length past sce:max-size, because the largest encoded size of a codec is computed from that bound and a decode that accepts more produces a value that breaks it; the generator is wrong and the generated documentation is right. Only the C11 arm of the generator's length-ref decode compares the length with the bound; the Rust, C++, Kotlin, Go and Python arms and the string variant do not, and the same gap holds for sce:max-count on the heap-backed repeat decode and on the encode side. wz therefore adds no check of its own in a wrapper and does not change the generated documentation: the fix is the generator's and wz regenerates out/** when the SCE session says it landed. The item stays open until then; this round records the answer so the carry names what it waits for.

Round 4056.decision_summary: Step 2 of decision D12 is built: the node's permit takes the commander. A closed type names who asks: the owner of the control pipe, a peer whose link's key proved a zid, or nobody shown. Every transport says which it is: the control port says the pipe, the in-band query says what the link proved, and a zid the sender merely claims is nobody. The compiled-in list of commanders is one list per verb, empty by default, naming only a verified zid; a zid listed for one verb commands no other, and a node commanded over a pipe as well gives the pipe every verb and the others to the list. Nothing a node does today changed: the write permit and the heap profile's key authority judge every commander alike, as they did, and an image that names its commanders gives the list in their place. Round 4057.decision_summary:
The 1 KiB host cell of the pico ABI moved from about half of zenoh-pico's rate to 86 percent of it, by a change in how many frames one write of a stream's queue may carry. One by one, wz read 190 k msg/s against pico's 360 k; it reads 310 k (wz to wz, and wz to pico) against 360 k. Round 4031 named the lever wrongly: it said the writer's role and the hop to its thread were the cost, and that a fix had to shorten what the writer holds. The reading below replaces that.

Measured on pc3 (TCP loopback peer, 1 KiB at 150,000 a second, no strace). Counted inside the library, the role was held by the writer for 98 percent of the frames that landed and the writer was parked for 2.4 percent of them, so the futex calls that strace showed (298,725 against pico's 14) were in good part strace's own doing and the hop is not the cost. The writer thread spent 91 percent of its CPU in the kernel, in `sendto`, and it wrote exactly one frame per write (1,037 bytes on average). The write was bounded by the link's batch, 2,048 bytes against a pico peer, and two frames weigh 2,074. A batch bounds one FRAME; a stream carries frames back to back, so how many leave in one write is invisible to the peer.

The change: `write_bound` in `crates/wz-runtime-tokio/src/writer_queue.rs`. A write is bounded by the link's batch, or by four frames of the first frame's size up to 64 KiB, whichever is more. A frame small against the batch is bounded as it was (a test pins thirty frames of 100 bytes to the batch). With the bound widened to 64 KiB for every size, a probe at 250,000 a second made the writer carry 3.8 frames a write and keep up, and the no-drop search read 260 k; the rule that was kept reads 310 k and leaves small frames exactly as they were, because nothing measured says a wider write helps them and a wider write holds more of the lane while it is written.

Not the lever, measured: a frame written by the thread that put it whenever the writer's role is free. It changed nothing (190 k), and the counters give the reason: 98.2 percent of the attempts found the role held, 14,032 of 1,200,000 wrote. It was dropped before any push.

Two things that move the figure and are not the library, read and recorded: the default pinning gives a process one SMT pair, and wz's sender and writer are two busy threads on it where pico is one (with two physical cores the unchanged writer read 290 k); and the 64 B figure read 4.48 M in one session and 4.32 M in the next with the unmodified queue too, one step of the search, so a difference of that size between sessions is the host's.

A peer's red is paid in this round: the close-ingress reason pin of `crates/wz-session-core/src/session_actions.rs` moved when D12 step 1 added `verified_peer_zid`, a read accessor; the reason's claims about `OutOfBand` and the requested close were re-read against the file and stand, and the row is moved. Two other reds (a released port in a re-dial test, a freshness check of the SHM namespace demo) were also repaired here and dropped from this round when the rebase showed another session had landed the same repairs first: origin should be fetched before a red is repaid.

What still parked a face's thread was the messages the stage did not take: the session core now probes a Declare, an Interest and a ResponseFinal as it probes a Push and a link-state message, each arm gated as its arm of the waiting send, and the router holds one that finds no room in the destination's data lane, behind what it holds, whoever sent it. A declaration can no longer reach a peer before held data that came first. A Request and a Response keep the waiting send (a shared-memory payload's handoff is not opened and given back by a probe yet), as does the session core's own permit for publish and the C ABI.

Round 4061.decision_summary: Three things, one cause. Upstream's regions test counts, for each node, the registrations it makes of a subscriber or a queryable, and a member of a multicast group registered the declaration of every other member twice where a publisher was declared: once for the member's announcement of its subscriber on the group (MulticastTxItem::Declare) and once for its answer to the interest the publisher asks the group (the answer a zenoh-pico member needs, which wz keeps). The registries of what a peer declared (RemoteSubscriberRegistry, RemoteQueryableRegistry) now keep a peer's declarations as a set of keyexprs, as upstream's hat holds one registration per face and resource (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/peer/pubsub.rs` @ `fn register_subscriber`): a keyexpr the peer declares again, under the same id or another, is not news (a queryable's change of completeness still is); both rows are kept, so either id withdraws it and the matching watches read what they read; the application is told the keyexpr gone when the last declaration of it goes, under the id it was told it by. Nothing on the wire changes. The second is a regression of round 4042 that the E7 mesh test found (wz_router_hat_federates_data_across_two_routers, reported with its bisect by another session): a router now tells a south peer only what it asked for, and a peer node's own publisher asked nothing (declare_local_interest only recorded the interest for the admin legs), so the demo's --publish peer never learned that a subscriber existed beyond its router. A peer node now sends the interest of its publisher or querier (current and future) to each router it is linked to and a Final when it goes, and sends the stored ones to a router that comes up later, as upstream's peer hat does (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/peer/interests.rs` @ `fn repropagate_interests`); the demo's --publish declares one before any face registers; a router, which has no router to ask, sends none. The third is the count: regions measured a process per test, 95 of 126 before the rebase and 94 after (one scenario 6 test reads a registration too many in about half the runs), against 78; scenarios 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 pass, scenario 1 needs the client node with a gateway, scenario 2 is peers that are gateways of their own regions, five of scenario 7 are intermittent. Round 4069.decision_summary:
The host table of the pico ABI gains the sizes between 64 B and 2 KiB, and the 2048 B cell is read. Up to 512 B wz is ahead of zenoh-pico (128 B: 2.64 M against 370 k msg/s; 256 B: 1.52 M against 370 k; 512 B: 680 k against 360 k), because one write of the stream's queue carries many frames where pico sends one per put. At 2048 B, a put past the 2,048 B batch (a chain of two fragments), wz read 125 k against pico's 185 k under the default pinning.

That deficit is placement, not the number of writes. Counted per thread under strace, pico makes two sendto calls a put (20,004 for 10,000 puts) and wz about one, the two fragments leaving in one write. At 120,000 a second wz's sender thread is 42 percent busy and its writer thread 86 percent, 82 percent of it in the kernel, and the default pinning puts both on one SMT pair. With the publisher given two physical cores, wz to wz reads 220 k against pico's 180 k (repetitions 220 k, 175 k, 220 k), so the cell is won when wz is given the CPUs its two threads need.

Two cells stay behind and are not explained by placement: 1 KiB (320 k wz to wz and 300 k wz to pico against 360 k) and 2048 B from wz to pico (160 k against 180 k). The common size of the gap, 11 to 17 percent, is a lead for the next reading, not a finding. No library code changed in this round.

Round 4071.decision_summary: The second link to a node is now refused while it is still being established, and no longer closed after it came up. Two peers that scout each other dial each other at once, and the two ends then admitted the link that completed first on their own side, exchanged declarations over it, and only when the rival came up closed the one the zid rule rejects (SharedSession::face_up in wz-capi-core, Admission::Replace). What crossed the closed link had been delivered to the application, and was delivered again over the kept one: the regions test of upstream read one registration too many for a queryable in about half the runs of scenario 6 (measured by tracing every link of a receiver: two links to the same remote zid, each told it once). Upstream decides at the handshake, the acceptor before it sends the OpenAck and the initiator before it sends the OpenSyn and again before it takes the OpenAck (`io/zenoh-transport/src/unicast/manager.rs` @ `init_transport_unicast`), so a refused link carries nothing in either direction. The node now does the same, as a collision is settled in BGP (RFC 4271 section 6.8) before the session is Established. A LinkAdmission (wz-session-core link_admission.rs) is installed on each link before its first wire byte and asked at three points of the handshake in the session core's drive.rs: the initiator at the InitAck, the acceptor at the OpenSyn, the initiator before the OpenAck is taken. A refusal sends Close(MaxLinks), the reason zenoh gives, and ends the open (DriverLoopOutcome::LinkRefused, OpenError::LinkRefused) with the FSM where it was, so the generated session machine is untouched. The node's table is LinkRegistry (wz-runtime-tokio link_registry.rs): a link already established keeps its place and a new one is refused, two links still in their handshakes that went the same way keep the first, and two that went opposite ways are decided by the zid rule that was already written (judge_second_link: the link the lower zid dialled is kept, the other is superseded and its initiator learns it before it declares anything). Only a link whose acceptor admitted it and whose initiator confirmed it carries a declaration, which the table's own test shows over every one of the 20 orders in which two crossed handshakes can interleave: exactly one link is up, never none and never two. The node that answers is the C API's peer (CApiForwarder, through FaceForwarder::link_admission, and the dial role's Dialer): its listener and its dials run in different loops over one registry, so only the registry sees the link another loop is bringing up. The router's own loop keeps its collision resolution, which decides after the link is up, and a loop that aggregates links (max_links above one) installs nothing. Round 4073.decision_summary: A router that hears of a peer from another peer before the peer's own entry reaches it kept an empty set of the peer's links for good, and two gateways of one region then both carried what only the primary should. The regions test of upstream (scenario 7: two routers and three peers to a region) read a sample twice at a subscriber in about a third of the runs of the five tests that show it (12 of 40). Traced by link and by verdict: the sample reached the subscriber from both gateways of its region, because the inter-region filter (`zenoh/src/net/routing/dispatcher/tables.rs` @ `impl InterRegionFilter<'_> {`) lets only the largest zid of the gateways a destination peer links to forward, and one router held none for that peer (gateways_of answered an empty list for the whole run, with the region's two gateways known) and the filter reads an empty list as "nothing to choose among, forward". The cause is the sn gate of the single-hop gossip ingest, which wz copies from upstream (`zenoh/src/net/protocol/network.rs` @ `fn process_singlehop_gossip_linkstate`): what a neighbour says of another node it knows is a zid and an sn and no links, and it sets the sn that the node's own entry, the only one that names its links, is later compared with; when the second-hand one arrives first (measured at the router: its first list from the peer read `new=0 updated=0` after a neighbour's list had already introduced the peer), the node's own entry carries the same sn and is dropped as not newer. Upstream has the same gate; its test runs on one worker thread, and here the order is the reading of how two handshakes interleave. The ingest now takes an entry of the SAME sn that names links when no entry of that sn has set the node's links yet (LinkstateNetwork keeps, for each node, the sn that last set them), which is no wider than it needs to be: the same sn is the same state, so what the entry adds is what a node that had heard it first would hold, and once the links are set the gate is upstream's again, so two nodes that announce each other do not do it forever (the same entry twice changes nothing, a test). An earlier form of the rule, for a node with no links at all, left the case of a node that holds the links of the sn before and hears of the next sn second-hand first (a router holding one gateway of a peer that links two was seen in an earlier trace); the rule keyed by the sn that set the links closes it. The residue is a different thing and is not closed here: a peer that links its second gateway raises its sn and tells the first gateway through a message of its own, and for the time that message takes the two gateways choose the primary among different sets (a router holding the peer's links as the first gateway alone, the other holding both), which is eventual consistency of the election and is upstream's too.

Round 4074.decision_summary:
The depth of the lane that the pico C ABI queues its frames on becomes a declared limit, PICO_TX_QUEUE_SIZE (Kconfig WZ_LIMIT_PICO_TX_QUEUE_SIZE), default 8; TxQueueConf::pico() reads it, clamped to upstream's 1..=16 for a queue size, and TxQueueConf::default() keeps upstream's 2. The 1 KiB and 2048 B cells of the host table, which stayed 11 to 17 percent behind zenoh-pico after round 4057, were bounded by this depth.

The reading: sampling the publisher at 1 KiB and 290,000 a second (150 stack samples under a debugger), the putting thread was in wait_for_room in 126 samples and the writer thread in epoll_wait in 148. A pico lane held two batches (4,096 bytes), so four 1 KiB frames filled it and the sender and the writer waited for each other after every four frames, bound by the wake latency of a futex and an eventfd. With the publisher on two physical cores, 1 KiB wz to wz and wz to pico read 320 k and 300 k at size 2, 540 k and 520 k at 4, 560 k and 960 k at 8, 560 k and 920 k at 16, against pico's 350 k to 360 k; 8 is the knee, so it is the default.

With the limit at 8 and the default pinning (one SMT pair), median of three on pc3: 1 KiB wz to wz 560 k, wz to pico 920 k, against 360 k; 2048 B wz to wz 230 k, wz to pico 480 k, against 180 k; 8 B and 64 B did not move (5.12 M and 4.48 M wz to wz, against 4.96 M and 4.32 M before, within one search step). Only the pico C ABI on the tokio engine reads the limit; the lwip and MCU paths use TxQueueConf::default() and are not touched.

The cost is stated and not hidden: wz spends about 27 percent more CPU than pico for the same rate (user time about five times), runs two threads where pico runs one, and a lane may now hold up to eight batches of heap while frames are queued. One host and loopback were measured, throughput only.

Round 4075.decision_summary: The acceptance criteria of the zenoh verdict, stated in groups. The thresholds are 2^-20 and a corpus cannot measure a rate that small: with no failure seen in n independent trials the 95% bound is about 3/n. Section 6.4 of the design note makes the claim in three layers: the theory (Ville) guarantees the nominal rate if the model is true and nothing tests it; the corpus tests the model at levels it can reach (2^-1 to 2^-10, the share of independent groups that cross each, with exact intervals) and the rate at 2^-20 is stated as an extrapolation; the cost is reported as expected sample size per group. Independence is counted in groups, the false no over zenoh groups and the false yes over null ones: claims of 10%, 5% and 1% need 29, 59 and 299 of each, and the corpus holds 22 and 18. A development corpus chooses the model; a validation corpus is collected after the model is frozen and fixed by a ledger entry before it is read. The levels are this session recommendation, not a ruling.

Round 4078.decision_summary:
Round 4074 stated that the wz side of the pico host table spends about 27 percent more CPU than zenoh-pico for the same rate, with about five times its user time. That statement is withdrawn: it was read from a run in which the publisher program spins between its 1 ms slots, a spin that is charged to the process and is long exactly when the library is faster than the offered rate, and the one wz reading was taken with a lane of two.

Read again with the spin replaced by a sleep (paced_pub -w), 1 KiB at 290,000 a second, a 4 s window of the per-thread ticks of /proc, lane at 8, two repetitions: pico's one thread 340 and 348 ticks of 400, wz's two threads together 231 and 236 (the sender 102 and 104, the writer 129 and 132). At that rate wz spends about a third less CPU than pico, mostly in the kernel, because it writes many frames in one call. Stack samples of the publisher agree: the writer thread was in epoll_wait in 194 of 200 samples, and the put path shows no single dominant function (memcpy is the top frame of none).

The split between user and kernel time is not stated: tick accounting put the writer's user time at 40 in one repetition and 0 in the other. The earlier claim that a vectored write or a zero-copy queue is the next lever is not supported by these readings and is dropped. The throughput figures of round 4074 are not affected: they come from the no-drop search, which does not use the sleep.

Round 4079.decision_summary: The first piece of the secure channel the fixed admin node lacks is built: the port a node accepts connections on. Zephyr's sockets now have a listener (`ZephyrTcpListener`, a `StreamListen` over bind, listen and accept, taken without blocking through `poll`), whose accepted connection is the same stream a connect gives. The IP stack gained `tls_acceptor`, the secure twin of `acceptor`: over a listener whose accept completes the channel's handshake (`TlsListener`) it yields the stack's `tls/` link, which carries the zid the peer's key proved, so the session host runs it as it runs a `tls/` dial. Until now an accepted connection could only become a `tcp/` link. Nothing binds the listener yet: the admin node over Zephyr's sockets, and the witness of a handshake on the target, are the pieces that remain.

Round 4088.decision_summary: Round 4073's hosted run (41292703209, tip 9c61dbcb8c) was red in eleven jobs, and every cause was the link admission of round 4071, which is mine; a peer session read the run and offered to repair it, and was told it is mine. Three causes, repaired here. (1) The heap-free tests of the fixed-memory crates (C1bnl, C1m: session_pool_exhaustion, host_acceptor_fixed_e2e, session_slot_allocations) counted one allocation per accepted handshake, asked for by wz-session-core. The cause was found by the peer from the accept arm of the guard in drive.rs: it read the remote's zid with peer_zid(), which copies it into a Vec, for every OpenSyn whether or not the node guarded the link, so a build with a heap paid for a question nobody asked. The guard now asks the lease first (link_admitted_for_remote) and copies the zid of a guarded link to a stack buffer, so no build allocates for it; the three tests pass. This also corrects the reading in round 4071's verification, which put the lwip no-heap tests down as unreachable by heap-gated code: the gate was the heap feature of the crate, and those tests build with it. (2) tests/link_admission_mutual_dial_e2e.rs was gated on routing-accept and transport-link-tcp but calls peer_loop, which the feature routing-peer configures in (C1al, two jobs); it is gated on all three. (3) Two doc links named LinkAdmission, which exists only with the heap: the module doc of link_admission.rs (a build without it has no item to link, now a code span) and the reference definition for confirm in link_registry.rs (now the full path); the reduced-configuration docs of wz-session-core pass in 124 configurations and those of wz-runtime-tokio in 138 (layer C1bzr of each crate alone, unsharded; the hosted shards and their settle are the verdict). Round 4073's verification also said that no router held an empty set of a peer's gateways in the traced runs. That was wrong: of four traced failing runs two showed routers judging a sample toward a peer with an empty set while both gateways of its region were known, one of them both routers. The retained trace shows why: a peer sent the declarations of its subscribers to a router before the list of its links (SharedSession::face_up replayed the declarations and then sent the gossip), so the router knew the subscriber and not the node, and the inter-region filter read an empty set as nothing to choose among and forwarded from every gateway. The peer now sends the gossip first: the link is FIFO, so whoever learns a declaration of the node has already learned its links, which is also the order upstream sends them in (Gossip::add_link on the creation of the link, declarations after it). Regions scenario 7 then fails 2 of 120 runs, against 7 before this order and 23 before round 4073; scenario 6 passes 30 of 30. The order is held by a test that decodes the frames a new face is sent (a_new_face_is_sent_its_topology_before_any_declaration), whose control with the replay first fails reading declaration, topology.

Round 4091.decision_summary:
The cause given for the pico lane depth in round 4074 is corrected. It said that the sender and the writer wait for each other after every four frames, bound by the wake latency of a futex and an eventfd. Three temporary changes of the queue, measured at 1 KiB with the publisher on two physical cores (two repetitions each), read otherwise.

Waking a sender only when the lane is at most half full left size 2 where it was (wz to wz 315 k, wz to pico 300 k against 320 k and 300 k): the wake rule is not the cause. Counting only the frames still queued, and not the batch the writer is writing, took size 2 to 560 k wz to wz and 590 k wz to pico: the cause is single buffering. A lane of two batches is full while the writer writes one, so the sender has no room until the writer asks for the next batch and production and writing do not overlap. With the same accounting at the default size 8 the lane read 570 k and 940 k, what size 8 reads unchanged (560 k and 960 k). What size 2 lacks even with the accounting, 590 k against 960 k to pico, is room to queue ahead of the writer, so the depth is a gain of its own.

Nothing was applied: the accounting adds nothing to size 8, and it would move the memory bound of a lane from what it holds to what is queued plus the batch being written. The limit PICO_TX_QUEUE_SIZE stays at 8 and keeps its meaning. The mechanism and the three rows are recorded in docs/upstream-parity.md, and the statement of round 4074 on the cause is withdrawn.

Round 4096.decision_summary: Step T4 of L6, the ABI: pico's tls/ opens on the cooperative engine through the exported z_* symbols. Four moves. (1) The PEM a Z_CONFIG_TLS_* key names is read by one crate, wz-tls-pem, which the tokio engine re-exports at its old paths and the pico ABI calls directly: the edge that holds the key spellings resolves path or base64 once, and no engine carries key-encoding knowledge. (2) CapiTlsConfig, the resolved material, is the port's value and wz-capi-core re-exports it; the rule that a client pair is whole or absent is the port's. (3) wz-capi-coop's tls-mbedtls feature gives tls::HostTls, the dial and the listen of a host stack made from that material. The channel was built for an image, and a host program that opens sessions over its life has none of what an image fixes, so the provider settles three things: the library starts on an arena of its own on first use, an identity and a set of roots are made once for each distinct PEM and lent for the program, and the time of each dial and accept is stated to the roots through Trust::set_now, new in this step, so a certificate that lapsed while the program ran is refused at the next handshake and not accepted for as long as the program lives. A pico program dials with its connect_* pair and listens with its listen_* pair and the channel's policy holds one identity, so the value holds a dial for each role. (4) pico's tls-mbedtls feature resolves the keys, gives the stack HostTls and selects the cooperative engine. Features add and the engines add with them (engine-tokio on is the tokio engine, as engine-coop beside it always was), so the choice is not a compile_error: that was built first and removed, because it broke --all-features and the gates built on it.

Round 4098.decision_summary: The suite tool that measures upstream's tests against the family (scripts/lib/z8_upstream_suite.py) could run each test of a file once, and the flake that round 4088 left in regions scenario 7 (2 of 120 runs) cannot be told from noise in one run. Z8_ONLY keeps the tests of the isolated file whose name contains the text (a scenario module, scenario7::) and Z8_REPEAT runs each that many times; both default to the whole file once, so the table of outcomes reads as before. With it the version-aware election that round 4088 named as the second candidate was built and measured, and it is not landed. The graph answered, for a node whose sn the net had heard of past the links it holds, every gateway of the net instead of the ones the node advertised (a unit test, and a control that the old answer was the first gateway alone). Scenario 7 then failed 2 of 200 runs without a trace and 5 of 200 with one, the same rate as 2 of 120 before it, and a trace of the crossing decision in the first failing run (the others were not read) shows why it cannot help: the router that forwards a second time holds the peer's links as current (a set of one gateway, no hearsay of a newer sn), and the peer's second link is simply not yet told to it. The sample is carried by the second gateway, which already has the peer's declaration over the new link, and by the first, which is told of the new link a message later over another connection; no sn or version in the first gateway's hands says so. Nothing in the protocol orders the two links, upstream has the same window, and closing it needs a hold or an acknowledgement the pin lacks. The election change is therefore reverted, with its trace, and what stays is the measuring tool.

verification_bullets: The selftest of the tool passes. Regions scenario 7 on a build machine (pc2), 200 runs of the 20 tests at ten each, through the tool with Z8_ONLY=scenario7:: and Z8_REPEAT=10: with the version-aware election 198 of 200 pass (two repeated timestamps, order 2 putsub), and 195 of 200 with the crossing trace on (order 2 pubsub, order 3 pubsub twice, order 2 putsub twice); the election was reverted after this. Not run: a measurement of the tree without the election at the same size, so the rate before is the 2 of 120 of round 4088; the hosted run; the capability cost gate.
carry_forward_bullets: Owed: regions scenario 7 still fails 1 to 2.5 percent of runs on a repeated timestamp (order 2 and 3, pubsub and putsub). The version-aware election is measured and does not move it, so it is off the list of candidates; what remains is a hold or an acknowledgement the pin lacks: a gateway that is told of a peer's second link a message after the second gateway carries a sample for it, over another connection. The decision is the owner's: close it with a hold (a gateway keeps a sample for a peer back until its view of the peer's links has been quiet for a short time), or record it as the pin's own window and leave the sample twice. The get and query timeouts of scenario 7 are not traced.

Owed, still: the hosted run of round 4088 and after (the run of its tip was cancelled by later pushes; the next uncancelled one is the verdict), the capability cost of the nine pico coop builds, Layer E whole.

Round 4099.decision_summary: The open of a link the node refused in its handshake no longer fails the node's connect. Since the link admission commit (c4e9a65195) a dial asks the node at the InitAck, and when a restarted peer dials a node whose old dialler dials it back at the same moment, the admission refuses one of the two links with MaxLinks; if the refused one was the open's own dial, session_open answered LinkRefused, which no caller read, so the C ABI mapped it to DriveFailed and the OnceThenFail arm failed the whole open, though the node was already linked to the one it dialled. The hosted wz-capi-pico mutual_dial test failed this way about one run in twenty. Dialer::open_or_held answers None for it and the first walk's arms read that as the connect met by the link the node holds; the redial of a lost link and every other caller still read it as a dial that did not open.

New test a_link_the_node_refuses_is_not_a_connect_that_failed against a handcrafted far end and an admission that refuses every link.

Round 4102.decision_summary: Step T4 of L6, the real programs: upstream's z_pub_tls and z_sub_tls run against the cooperative engine and pass in both directions, the two legs that Layer E skipped by name while the engine had no tls/ link. Measured, in order. The certificates those examples carry are RSA-2048 (a minica root, an end certificate signed sha256WithRSAEncryption, a PKCS#1 RSA PRIVATE KEY) and the channel's Mbed TLS built P-256 and ECDSA only, so both legs failed in z_open at once and the example says only "Unable to open session!". The crate's rsa feature gives the host RSA keys, RSA signatures read to verify a chain and RSA-PSS, and a 600 byte public key buffer in place of 160; it is the host's, the kit image configures the channel by Kconfig and never sets it, so the kit is unchanged, and wz-capi-coop's tls-mbedtls turns it on. With that both legs failed again, now in the handshake. OpenSSL, run against the same chain in both directions, named the cause: dialling got no suitable signature algorithm and accepting ended in alert 40. TLS 1.3 signs a handshake with an RSA key by RSA-PSS, and Mbed TLS's TLS layer lists rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 in its signature algorithms only when MBEDTLS_X509_RSASSA_PSS_SUPPORT is defined, which the crypto side's PSA_WANT_ALG_RSA_PSS does not do; that macro is in turn refused by Mbed TLS's own configuration check without PSA_WANT_ALG_RSA_OAEP, which the channel does not use and now carries for that reason. After it OpenSSL negotiated TLSv1.3 with TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and verified the chain both ways, and the two real-program legs pass. TLS 1.3 alone served upstream's examples as built (Mbed TLS 3.6.4 with 1.2 and 1.3 on, against a channel that speaks 1.3 only). Layer E and Layer Z, which build one artifact path, build the cooperative library with tls-mbedtls, the sweep no longer skips tls, and its count is 32.

Round 4107.decision_summary: The verbs of the admin node on Zephyr's sockets are witnessed through the query transport on the target. In deploy/zephyr-admin-loopback the fixed-memory client, which dials the admin node over tls/, now asks two GETs through its session: session/status/<peer> and session/close/<peer> under the node's zid. The status its key is listed for is answered with a status document, and the close it is not listed for is refused by name, so the zid the node decided by is the one the session's key proved and the plumbing of the requester (decision D12 step 1) carries it through a real session. The pair discriminates both ways: an unproven requester would be refused the status, and a node that took the requester for anyone would answer the close. Round 4108.decision_summary: A consumer measured that a gap on a multicast group link is never counted: the passive reader set the SN ring only from an InitAck, so every Frame and Fragment of a UDP multicast or raweth flow read without_resolution. On a link with no handshake each sender's JOIN now states the ring its SNs are judged on (S clear states the defaults) and where they start: every conduit holds next_sn minus one, per priority under QoS, as upstream's receiver syncs a peer it learns. A later JOIN of the same sender moves nothing; one naming another zid, ring, role, lease or QoS starts the sender again. Rings are per direction, so two senders on one flow are judged apart. A JOIN on a link with a handshake is inadmissible and folds nothing. Field document 48 and census 22 record the moved values; no key moves.

Round 4115.decision_summary: The open of a link the other end refused no longer fails the node's connect. Round 4099 made a link the node itself refuses in its handshake (LinkAdmission) read as the node held by another link; the hosted wz-capi-pico mutual_dial test still failed on hkl002 afterwards, with the same -128. The other path is the accepting end's refusal: when a restarted peer and an old dialler cross, the end that holds the other link answers the InitSyn or the OpenSyn with Close(MAX_LINKS), which the dialling end read as a plain terminal handshake and the C ABI as DriveFailed. A Close with that reason before Established now ends the drive as LinkRefused, after the FSM has taken it, so the same Dialer::open_or_held answers None for it, as upstream's open.rs and accept.rs treat MAX_LINKS (a debug log, not a fault). A Close in an Established session is unchanged.

Round 4121.decision_summary: Round 4098 left regions scenario 7 failing 1 to 2.5 percent of runs on a repeated timestamp and named the cause as a window the protocol does not order: a peer that links a second gateway sends its declarations over the new link while its announcement of that link, sent over the first, is still in flight, so the first gateway still holds the peer's links as itself alone and both gateways elect themselves primary and carry one sample twice. That round left open whether to close the window with a hold or record it as upstream's own. This round closes it with a barrier, and the answer to the open question is that the window is closed, bounded, and costs the dialling side one round trip. A first experiment confirmed the cause before any design: holding the declaration replay of a dialled second link for a fixed 100 ms gave 0 failures in 600 runs against about 1.4 percent without it. The barrier replaces the fixed delay by what the delay stood for. A dialled link is announced first (the gossip send to every other face that hears of a link); then the dialling side asks each of those faces a liveliness get on a reserved key and waits for the final of the answer, which on a link that keeps order comes after the announcement was handled; only then are the declarations replayed over the new link, and a bound of 1000 ms ends the wait if a face never answers. The wait is an await, not a blocked thread: the first attempt blocked the drive thread and was wrong twice over, since the runtime refuses a blocking section on a local task set and, on the serial drive, the very tasks that read the answer run on the same thread. The accepting side keeps the unbarriered face_up, since it cannot await in its synchronous trait and the dialling side is the one whose announcement races its declarations. During the wait the face is already in the registry with empty tables and owes nothing yet; the first await version left it out and dropped the gossip sent to it, which failed 40 of 400 runs, ten times the baseline, and the replay then skips whatever the registry declared to the face in the meantime. Measured on a build machine through the suite tool with Z8_ONLY=scenario7:: and Z8_REPEAT: 1200 runs of scenario 7 failed 4 times (0.33 percent) against about 17 expected at 1.4 percent; 200 runs of scenario 6 all passed. The barrier does not reach zero: 2 of the 4 failures are the repeated timestamp and 2 are an equality assertion of a queque test whose cause is not attributed. Corrections to earlier entries arrive here, not in them: round 4098 said the window was closed only by an owner's hold; it is closed by an acknowledgement the family can ask for with its own liveliness get, no pin change.

Round 4122.decision_summary: The listener of Zephyr's sockets sets SO_REUSEADDR before it binds, as the POSIX listener does, so a node restarted on its port is not kept off it by the connection the earlier listener closed first. The witness is in deploy/zephyr-tls-loopback: a listener serves one connection, closes it first and goes, and a listener on the same port must bind at once. It discriminates: with the option applied the image prints that the restarted listener took the port and Layer Qz passes, with the option never applied the same image fails with a refused bind (Bind(-1)). Building the witness showed a second limit of the image that the product images will meet when they restart: Zephyr's TCP side of a context is a connection object from a pool of CONFIG_NET_MAX_CONN (4 on an IPv4-only build, not CONFIG_NET_MAX_CONTEXTS), a closed connection keeps its slot in TIME_WAIT, and a listen with no free object is refused (-1); the witness image states 16. The product admin image states CONFIG_NET_MAX_CONTEXTS only and keeps the default of 4 connections; whether a restart under load needs more is not measured and is not changed here.

Round 4128.decision_summary: L6 carry items after round 4112, measured, and one fixed: the host build of the secure channel held 7 sessions, not the 198 its arena takes. The publisher a router dials: a zenoh (Rust) peer publisher, listening and dialed by a real zenohd, reaches a pico z_sub client behind the router in 2.5 s, because it sends Interest(CurrentFuture, keyexprs and subscribers) for its publisher's key as soon as the link is up and the router answers by propagating the client's subscriber to it. The real pico z_pub and wz's pico drop-in z_pub send neither that Interest nor a Push to the router. That is pico's rule and the drop-in keeps it on purpose: a pico peer asks only while it holds a router as a peer at the time it declares, and here it declares before the router dials. It is therefore not a defect of wz's channel or of the drop-in's parity, and no test pins it, since a test of nothing delivered would hold wz to pico where wz may do better. Round 4112 said the suite has no built Rust example; that was wrong, scripts/build-zenohd.sh installs zenoh_z_pub beside zenohd. TLS 1.2: a client offering 1.2 only is refused with the protocol_version alert and the listener sees nothing to accept; the channel has 1.3 only by design. The arena against a count of sessions: a held server session takes about 20 KB with an RSA-2048 certificate and the 4 MiB arena takes 198 of them, but what bound a program first was the PSA key store, which the library sizes to 32 keys by default and an established session holds four of (7 sessions held, the eighth handshake dropped without a word, 4 MiB unused). The host build (feature host-lock) now sizes the store to 1024; the kit image sizes it by Kconfig and is untouched. The examples' certificates are valid from 2023 to 2123, so no leg depends on a date.

Round 4134.decision_summary:
The host throughput comparison is extended from the pico family to the zenoh-c family: the same publisher and subscriber sources are built against the zenoh-c 1.10.2 release and against wz-capi-c (scripts/pico-compare.sh nodrop-c, with one compatibility header for the two C APIs), and the 64 B and 1 KiB cells are recorded. The 8 B cells with wz in them are not stated: a measured loss at the end of a run, not the rate, stops them.

The loss was found by changing one thing at a time. A wz publisher dropped before its session loses the last 500 to 1100 puts in 4 to 16 of 20 runs at 400 k/s; left to the session drop, or after a pause of 5 ms, it loses none. The undeclare of the publisher's key (Control) overtakes the queued puts (Data) on the writer lanes and the peer, which has unregistered the alias, drops them. The barrier in the lanes that is built and not landed (fence-wip) removes the loss in the same test, 0 of 20. This round does not land it: its owner is reading an unrelated race that it makes likelier. A flush of the open batch frame before the seal was tried first and changed nothing, and was not kept.

Round 4135.decision_summary: The replay fuzz target found that wz_replay_mutate ended its caller's process for an EXTEND by a count no memory holds: the door built the mutated payload on the heap to learn its length and only then compared it with the caller's buffer. Mutation::bytes is the one definition of the mutated bytes: apply_into writes it and changes compares it, so the door has no formula of its own. The three inputs the fuzzer wrote are seeds of every replay, as base64 in fuzz_seeds.py.

Round 4137.decision_summary: Repays the residue round 4132 carried: a Response or a ResponseFinal that arrived in fragments named no request, its above_transport.carried entry writing null where its unfragmented twin writes the pairing. The exchange plane already folds a completed chain's records at the fragment that completed it, so the pairing existed and only the renderer withheld it. Those entries now carry closes and answers from the same pairing, keyed by the completing row and the record's place in the joined batch; a fragment row carries no records of its own, so the places do not collide. A request that arrived in a chain is named by that row's seq and its place in that row's above_transport.carried. Round 4139.decision_summary: Two carry items of round 4128 paid. (1) Identity::from_pem refused an RSA private key written as PKCS#8 (BEGIN PRIVATE KEY, what OpenSSL 3 writes by default) with PSA's invalid-argument code, -135, while the same key as PKCS#1 opened. Cause, read in the pinned Mbed TLS: the PKCS#8 branch for RSA in mbedtls_pk_parse_key sets the private key and never the public half, which its PKCS#1 branches do set, and mbedtls_pk_check_pair returns the invalid-argument code for a context with no public half. The library is pinned and not edited; the channel writes every RSA key out as PKCS#1 DER and reads it back once at load (pk_complete_public, under the rsa feature). A first probe that asked whether the public half was set was wrong: mbedtls_pk_write_pubkey_der answers an empty key with the wrapper of an empty key and a positive length, so the fix does not ask. Elliptic-curve keys in PKCS#8 were never affected. (2) A handshake the listener ended without a stream was seen by the caller of accept only as nothing to accept, which hid an arena or a key store with no room. TlsListener now counts them (dropped) and keeps the channel's error of the latest that had one (last_drop); a stall past the accept budget is counted and has no error. The C ABI's listener is boxed behind TlsDial::listen, so a C program does not read the counters yet.

Round 4141.decision_summary:
Upstream's liveliness test regression_1 failed on wz at 3599 (a subscriber got a sample before the token was undeclared) in 4 of 300 runs on a tree that also holds the control-frame fence, and in none of 105 without it. The fence only moved the timing; the race was already there.

Cause, read from the debug log of the failing runs: a peer node and the router node it joins keep their links through RouterForwarder, which did not implement FaceForwarder::link_admission. The default is None, so the handshake never asked the node whether a second link to a held node may carry anything. Two peers that dial each other (the configured endpoint on one side, the autoconnect of the gossip on the other) made three links; all three came up as faces, the first one replayed its declarations, and then the accept loop's decision after the link is up closed face 1 for the link the lower zid dialled. Closing face 1 retracted the token its peer had declared on it (the application was told a Delete) and the replacing face declared it again (a Put). Only the C ABI's own forwarder (CApiForwarder) answered the admission, which is why the registry and its twenty-order model test existed and the router nodes did not use them.

The repair is the textbook one for a connection collision (RFC 4271 section 6.8, and the handshake-time decision upstream makes in its transport manager): decide while the link is still being established. RouterForwarder now owns a LinkRegistry built from its own zid and answers link_admission with it, so an established link keeps its place, of two links still in their handshake the one the lower zid dialled wins, and the loser is closed with MaxLinks before either end declared anything over it. A face leaving releases its place at once (release_link_admission in deregister), as the C ABI's registry does, so a node that comes back is not refused for the link that left. The decision after the link is up stays for a link that came up while no rival was known and for a loop that aggregates links.

The loop-level test of two routers dialling each other asserted that the lower zid's link is always the one kept, which was what the decision after the link is up gave and is not what the handshake gives: a link that is already established keeps its place. It now asserts what matters to an application: one face each, the same link at both ends, and one FaceUp with no FaceDown at each node.

Every queued frame now carries an enqueue number, the session raises a fence on the link after the barrier flush, and the Control lane waits while a lane holds an entry numbered below the fence. A session with no QoS keeps one lane and is not held. The reconnect seam forwards the fence to the live link. The race it exposed in the upstream liveliness test (a face replaced after crossing dials) was repaired by link admission in the handshake, and the test passes 200 of 200 with the fence.

Round 4143.decision_summary: The carry item "how pico itself settles a certificate's dates" is answered by reading. In the pinned zenoh-pico, the TLS stream refuses a handshake whose verify result holds any flag outside a short ignore list: a name mismatch on a dial that did not ask for the name check, and a skipped verification on a listener without mutual TLS. Expired and not-yet-valid are not on it, so a lapsed certificate is refused, provided the platform's Mbed TLS reports dates at all: BADCERT_EXPIRED is set only under MBEDTLS_HAVE_TIME_DATE in the pinned Mbed TLS. The provider states the host's wall time at each dial and refuses a lapsed certificate (tls_provider), so the two agree on a host; a pico build without a clock checks no date, which is its platform's property and not a mode the provider offers.

Round 4147.decision_summary: The cooperative engine now decides a second link to a held node in the link's handshake, as the tokio nodes do, instead of after both ends have brought it up. The table behind the decision moved into wz-session-core (LinkBook, and LinkRegistry over the runtime's own lock) so that one table answers for every engine; the tokio registry is an alias of it. Each cooperative link takes a lease before its handshake runs, an established link keeps its place, and of two links still in their handshake the one the lower zid dialled is kept. The face swap after the handshake (admission, displace) is gone: the engine builds only where pointer atomics exist, so the branch for a target without them could not be compiled. The dial role's face that a node refused stands by until no other face reaches that node, read from the face table at each step, so a link that dies in its handshake frees the node as well.

Round 4148.decision_summary:
A session that closes while its data plane holds an open frame no longer drops that frame. Small puts are staged into the open frame of their priority and the link's writer puts it on the wire when it falls idle, through a hook that holds the session weakly; OpenedSession::drain_to_close let go of the session first, so a close that came before the writer's idle flush found the hook empty and the frame was dropped with the session. The puts of the last milliseconds of a burst had returned Z_OK and never arrived. drain_to_close now hands the open frames to the writer (batch_flush) before it lets go, and the seal that follows drains them.

This is a second cause beside the one recorded in the host comparison round. The undeclare of a dropped publisher is a Control barrier that already hands the open frame over, and then overtakes it on the writer lanes (the barrier in the lanes, landed since, holds it back). A close with no undeclare has no barrier, and the open frame was lost. The earlier statement that a close left to the session loses nothing was a reading of timing on that tree, not of the code, and is withdrawn.
