Round 4330.decision_summary: The admission property of a stream link is the seventh step of the stream suite: HW.42, a peer past the node's capacity does not harm the sessions it holds, and the node takes its peer back once it has gone. A first draft judged only that the sessions survived and the node recovered, and a probe of the real node showed that was too little: it stood eight idle connections at the node's listener on QEMU's forward and watched them, and six were closed by the node within half a second while two stayed idle until it reaped them between three and six seconds, so the node refuses what it cannot hold, promptly, and holds two (the cell it keeps for a connection waiting to be taken and the one handshake it reads at once, QUEUE and ACCEPTS in its source). The step now judges that: it stands five idle connections straight at the listener (not through the proxy, which would stall its own accept loop on a listener that drops what it cannot take), waits as events for the node to close the ones it cannot hold, and requires that at most the capacity of two still stood at two seconds, which is below the reap, so a refusal is told from a reaping. While they stand a query through A (a held session carrying a request and its reply) must be answered with both sessions and B must still report both; closing them must give their cells back, which one release of A and its return show. The capacity is derived from the contract, the accepts constant joins the drift check, and the step's comparison is one pure function with four model faults: a session taken down to make room, a cell kept after the connection is gone, a pressure that never lands and a node that holds every connection.

Round 4332.decision_summary: The sustained property of a stream link is the eighth step of the stream suite: HW.43, a long run of queries is answered whole, one after another, and the node's sessions and cells are as they were after it. What a run of a few queries cannot show is a table that loses an entry now and then, a counter that does not carry, a session whose timer the queries never renew, and a pool that shrinks while every answer is right; the step asks through router A, a request to the node and its reply across the leg to A, for as many queries as the largest fixed table the node holds (its four timers, held to the node's source by the drift check) times five hundred, so a node that loses one entry in four hundred queries or faster has none left before the run ends, and the count is far past the 128 a one-byte request number holds. The run stops at the first query that is not answered with both sessions, so a node that has stopped answering costs one guard and not one for each query left. After it, router B must still report both sessions, and one release of A and its return show the pool whole: a session that ends after the run and a cell the run lost are each found there and nowhere else. The comparison is one pure function and has no clock; the time is measured and printed. The step is not run when HW.42 did not hold, because a pool that step found short would fail this one for that step's reason. Four model faults, each reds this step alone: a table entry leaked now and then until the node answers no more, an answer that names the wrong sessions past a count, cells of the pool lost to the run with every answer right, and a session lost after the run with every answer right; each comparison weakened to drop one clause lets its fault go green. The drift check is now held by a mutation of each constant it reads (timers, accepts, sessions, cells, lease).

Round 4333.decision_summary: Coalescing is the other half of framing and the ninth step of the stream suite: HW.44, several requests that arrive in one read are each answered whole, and the node's sessions are as they were. HW.41 cuts one message into many reads; this joins many messages into one. The leg to A is held (the proxy buffers what router A sends the node and forwards nothing), eight requests are made through router A together, and the buffer is then sent as one write. Eight is more than one and few enough to fit the node's batch at 128 bytes each. The barrier that shows every request arrived is the buffer's content and neither a size nor a time: each request carries a tag of its own in its selector, which router A passes on as it is, and the wait is for every tag to be in what the proxy buffered, on the proxy's condition and to a guard below the lease, so the keep-alives that also cross the held leg cannot stand in for a request (a byte count would have let them). The proxy's hold was reworked for it: the state is per connection and per direction under that direction's lock, and a release ends the hold and sends the buffer in one step, so a read landing between the two is neither sent ahead of the buffer nor stranded in it, and it returns the writes that call made, so a write made by a later read cannot be taken for the buffer's. The log of what was buffered is kept as it was read. The comparison is one pure function (requests made, every tag buffered, exactly one write, every answer both sessions, both sessions held afterwards); five model faults each red it alone (a tail of the read dropped, a wrong reply, requests never handed over together, a request that never reached the buffer, a session reset after right answers), and each comparison weakened to drop one clause lets its fault go green. The batch joins the drift check, for the one node that states it as a constant. The step is not run when HW.42 did not hold.

The verdict program's selftest passes. Round 4336.decision_summary: Phase 6 of docs/router-table-snapshots.md (section 6.3). A second instrument times the writes of an admission by band of faces already up and the copy of each store: on the tree of phase 5 a write under snapshot at 2048 faces cost 2.5 times rwlock's for a subscription (1313 against 521 us) and 4.6 times for an interest (602 against 130 us), almost all of it whole copies of the future-subscription store and the broker hat's client subscriptions (191 to 398 us each). Those stores are now persistent maps (a hash array mapped trie written for the router, Bagwell 2001) whose writers read first and write only what changes; after it, at 2048 faces, 968 against 935 us and 256 against 227 us, every store's copy 0 us but the face map's 10 us. The starved router's bring-up still failed, and a bring-up timeline showed why: every session that came up did so in the first 10 s (the accept timeout) and none after, under rwlock as well (2048, 1451, 1350 of 2048 against snapshot's 1773, 1056, 1324 as the host's load went from 2 to 9), because the harness started the router on one core at nice 10 instead of moving it there once its sessions were in, as its own comment said. With the harness corrected, E7s passed every test in two alternating runs of each value at host loads of 3 to 30, per message within the spread of either value; with no writer the instrument's readers route within 2.6 per cent of rwlock's, so the outermost read keeps its count. Snapshot is the recommended value for a router whose sessions come and go; the default stays rwlock, as C2 requires of every policy.

Round 4341.decision_summary: A board row's verdict_steps names the steps its record was made against, and it could name one step or one range. A stream node's steps are not one range: HW.0 to HW.7 are every node's, HW.8 to HW.25 are the second interface's, HW.26 to HW.35 are the datagram pools', and HW.36 to HW.44 are what only a stream suffers, so the row of the node over tcp/ could not name what it has run without naming steps its image does not carry. The scope is now one or more step expressions joined by ' and ', each a step or a range, in ascending order without overlap: the order and the no-overlap are what give a scope a single spelling, so the witness's verdict text can be held to the same words as before (the first step expression it opens with must be the scope itself, so a record that names only the first range does not stand for a scope of two). Every step inside every range is still read as before: published by the grammar, named in the entry, OK and not FAIL. The narrowing remains a narrowing of what the record must name, and not a way round the grammar.

Round 4346.decision_summary: The router's interests and the broker hat's subscriptions are indexed by keyexpr: KeyexprIndex, a persistent trie of keyexpr chunks (path-copied like the phase 6 maps), finds the members whose keyexpr may meet a question, wildcards on either side, and the exact matcher the scan used decides each candidate (filter and refine), so every answer is the scan's. The broker hat's exact-key questions (sub_contributions, sub_keys, the re-declare check) read the store's index by key instead of trying every face. Round 4348.decision_summary: A querier of a lifecycle verb is declared by its words, not its key: verb, of (the zid of one of the node's peer endpoints), about (a zid or self), whatami (client unless stated), generation for reset, mode for open; one of key and verb. The generator makes the key as lifecycle_wire::VerbKey reads it, so no declaration and no consumer spells the key grammar, and raises the node's key budget to the longest key such a querier can ask. about = self is the node's own zid, a fact of the node when it runs (its [identity] or a key it makes at start), so the key is generated up to its last chunk and the node ends it at start through slot_querier::LaunchedKeys (written once before the node exists, read as the 'static key a Query asks). The node says each querier's key at start, HOST-WZ-QUERIER <n> <key>, so a consumer joins the ASKED, REPLY and VERDICT lines to the querier by its place in the declaration.

Round 4355.decision_summary: The verdict-leg mutation job (Layer C0mut) has been cancelled at its 30 minute limit in every hosted run read since R3140, grading nothing, and the two shards of R4245 did not end it: in run 42182407682 shard 0 was one mutant short of its 42 and shard 1 had run 17 of about 39. The cost is not spread by the legs. A leg whose killing test is in wz-replay makes each of its three mutants run that crate's whole suite, 189 s on one runner and 393 s on a slower one, against 8 to 12 s for a leg wz-capture kills, and each shard first spends 3.6 to 7.4 minutes on its baseline. The legs are taken in sorted order and shard k asks those at positions congruent to k, so at two shards the heavy legs known (GapsForced at 13, PacketsSkipped at 14, SnMissing at 20) sat in shards 1, 0 and 0 and at four they sit in 1, 2 and 0. The matrix becomes [0, 1, 2, 3] with WZ_MUTANTS_SHARDS 4 and the job name says /4; the predicate thresholds spread 9, 8, 8, 8. The timeout moves from 30 to 60 minutes: a shard holding one heavy leg and a quarter of the rest reads about 32 minutes on the slow runner and one holding two about 50, and a cancel grades nothing, so the number is not tight. Not done, because it is the way out only if measured: making a mutant run fewer tests of wz-replay; a kill is found by the first failing test but libtest runs the binary to its end. The positions of the other legs (PayloadGaps, ThroughputGaps) are not known to be heavy; the next run that ends shows each shard's length.

Round 4357.decision_summary: bx's per-unit requirement form was installed on all seven fleet hosts on 2026-11-07, so a check unit can now say what its lane fails without, and bx gives it only to a machine that has it. A requirement is something the LANE fails without, not something its hosted job happens to install. Packages were first read from each job's apt steps. Asked with that set, every machine that answered lacked liblz4-dev and libsnappy-dev, which would have placed 114 lanes nowhere, and those lanes had passed on those machines. That reading was dropped. Requirements now come from where the tree states the lane's dependence. An arming in the lane's function maps to the oracles armed_oracle_census.py declares for it: a program becomes `needs`, and a file or module becomes the Debian package that provides it (a new PROVIDED_BY map, drift-guarded like the rows). A lane whose function uses netns-sandbox.sh asks `userns-net-raw`. Two hosted-job-armed programs (U's gh, C1cc's valgrind) are written in the planner with the lanes' failure sentences. C1bs could hold CAP_NET_RAW only by itself or through sudo, so it now falls back to the namespace sandbox the way Layer M does, with the live arm's feeder inside the same namespace as the tap. bx's `userns-net-raw` tests NET_RAW alone, while the sandbox also takes NET_ADMIN and SYS_ADMIN; the planner says so, and an exact capability is the fleet owner's decision.
changes_bullets: scripts/lib/runci_plan.py: plan lines carry `needs`, `packages` and `capabilities` when a lane asks something (7 of 180 do), read by `lane_asks` from each lane's function (census armings, the sandbox) and JOB_ARMED_COMMANDS (U: gh, C1cc: valgrind). A JOB_ARMED_COMMANDS entry for a lane the table lacks is refused. The docstring records why a job's apt packages are not requirements, and the selftest covers both sources (10 cases). scripts/lib/armed_oracle_census.py: PROVIDED_BY maps each file and python-module oracle to its Debian package, and `requirements(flag)` returns what a machine is asked for. `--check` refuses an oracle with no package and a package for an oracle no row names, and the selftest drives both. scripts/run-ci.sh: Layer C1bs tries the namespace sandbox after its own capability and sudo (a broken sandbox fails, an absent one skips or fails under the flag), and its live arm runs feeder and tap together through `_c1bs_live_read`. docs/verdicts-in-the-fleet.md: stage 3 records the requirements and what is left.
verification_bullets: `bx --checks ci --only C1bs,C1cc,C1bn,U` in the fleet gave 2 pass, 0 fail and 2 not measured. C1bn passed on hkl002 (315 s), placed away from hkl001, which lacks libpcap-dev and protoc. C1bs passed on hkl002 (27 s) under WZ_LIVECAP_REQUIRE=1, where only the sandbox could hold CAP_NET_RAW, and a skip there would have been a failure. U was not measured: "hkl001 lacks the command gh; hkl002 lacks the command gh; pc2 lacks the command gh". C1cc was not measured twice, because only pc2 has valgrind and pc2 was held by other runs. `bx --explain-candidates` with the narrowed set reported each machine's gaps, and none of the 173 units that ask nothing is affected. The planner selftest passed 10 cases and `--check` planned 180 lanes. The census selftest refused all 6 damage probes plus the stale package for their own reasons, and `--check` reported 11 oracles. shellcheck 0.11.0 was clean on run-ci.sh.
carry_forward_bullets: Stage 3 waits on fleet provisioning, not on the tree. U needs gh and an API token in the fleet run account, and C1cc needs valgrind on more than one machine (or a free pc2); both are the owner's. A capability tested exactly as the namespace sandbox is used (NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN and NET_RAW plus a veth pair) is with the fleet's owner. After that, run the whole set again. C1's get-timeout stays unattributed (300 of 300 clean on a build machine). Read the next hosted run per job.

The demo is now built at its default features at the head of the lane, before the first leg that reads it; the legs further down that need another feature set already build it themselves.

The phase 6 instrument, extended to time a queryable, an interest in queryables and a token per admitted client, found two more costs that grew with the faces up: every registration reconciled every token against each mesh link, a client's too although it moves no graph (94 to 99 ms per registration at 2,048 faces), and the forwarder's record of what it told each region of tokens was a hash map of hash sets that a token declaration under snapshot copied whole. The linkstate tables' register and deregister now say whether the face moved a graph and only such a face reconciles, and the record is a persistent map of persistent sets, read before it is written. Under snapshot the last per-face cost of a declaration is the face map's spine, carried.

Round 4362.decision_summary: The datagram pool steps now run on the kit. The kit lane captured the console of the node under test and ran the program's board mode against it for the steps every node has, HW.0 to HW.7, and for a stream node the stream steps; the pool steps, HW.26 to HW.35, judged from the same console, the program's own output and a capture of the node's frames, were run by hand on the bench in round 3315 and by no lane since. The lane now starts a capture of the frames to and from the node's address at the host's wire before the reset, and for an image built with a pool (the table says which, as POOLS) it puts the run to that pool's steps once the program's output is written. Making that run stand on its own found two faults of the lane's reading, which are fixed because a lane that is right three times and wrong a fourth is not a verdict. First, the directory of a built image is the same for every run of it, so a file a run waits on (a READY line in the console, 'listening on' in the capture's output) was read from the run before when the wait came before the process that writes the file had truncated it; the first run of the pool image was judged on the previous boot's READY line, whose node id the node under test did not have, and the run's own steps failed on it. A run now removes the console, capture, reset and verdict files of the run before it before it does anything, and the boot under test is cut from the console at the first Zephyr banner after the reset, which is told by the console and not by a clock. Second, a capture is ended by a signal sudo hands to its command only once the command runs; a signal sent in the first moments after the start was taken by sudo and lost, and the lane waited on the capture for ever. The signal is now sent until the capture has gone, and a capture that cannot be ended is said to be.

Three runs, each flashed and reset again, held the eighteen steps, the console held no failure line in any of them, and each was inside its budget row (the stack line at 13,736 of 65,536 bytes in all three, as in the budget row). Round 4364.decision_summary: Layer U asked two questions in one command. Its verdict on the tree is whether the pins agree with what upstream had published, and whether the workflow's cache keys and toolchain agree with the pins. Whether upstream has published since is a fact about the world, not about any commit. Because the lane called the releases API itself, one commit could be green one day and red the next, a machine without gh and a token could not judge it, and the fleet placed it nowhere. The fleet's owner recommended splitting it rather than handing the fleet a token. The API's answer is now an input the tree carries: scripts/lib/upstream_releases.json, written by `upstream_release_distance.py --fetch` where gh is authenticated, holding each derived repository's releases and each pinned ref's toolchain channel, with the sha256 of that body. Layer U reads only that file. Item 578's condition 3 holds on both sides. The verdict fails on a snapshot that is absent, does not match its digest, or is silent about a repository or pin the tree now names, so a pin bump refreshes the snapshot in the same commit. `--watch` compares the snapshot with the live API on a daily schedule (upstream-watch.yml), outside the check set, and fails when upstream has moved or cannot be read. The fleet's C0 run of this change then failed in the fault proxy's own stress cases, which run on every C0. Measured on a loaded build machine, two defects showed. A reject's reset can reach the client at its connect rather than its first read, and the case allowed only the read. The proxy's release ended the hold one direction at a time, so the reply to what it sent up landed in the still-held down direction and was returned as the buffer's own. The release now ends both directions and sends both buffers in one step under both locks.
changes_bullets: scripts/lib/upstream_release_distance.py: `--fetch` writes the snapshot from the live API and writes nothing if any read fails (a toolchain read that is not a 404 is a failure). `--watch` compares the snapshot with the live API and fails on any difference or an unreachable API. The default verdict serves `run` from the snapshot through `snapshot_fetchers`, which names stale entries and raises SnapshotStale for missing ones. `declared_toolchains` fails a pin the snapshot does not answer for. The selftest adds 13 snapshot cases. scripts/lib/upstream_releases.json: the snapshot (9 repositories, 7 pinned refs). .github/workflows/upstream-watch.yml: a daily `--watch` with GITHUB_TOKEN. ci.yml: Layer U has no token. run-ci.sh: Layer U has no gh check. runci_plan.py: U no longer asks for gh. round_fed_gate_reach.py, hook_default_region_gate.py, bump_sweep.py, docs/agent-reference.md and docs/verdicts-in-the-fleet.md: Layer U is described as reading the snapshot. scripts/lib/stream_fault.py: `_Pair.flush` ends the hold and sends both directions under both locks. The reject case accepts a reset seen at connect. An unexpected error in the cases names its line.

Round 4367.decision_summary:
A Zephyr image can now state the policies it reads. Until this round the image's build passed the limits to cargo (WZ_LIMIT_*) and no policy, and its Kconfig tree did not hold Kconfig.policies, so a policy could be set in the host flow only. The declaration now says, per image, which policies the image's code reads ([[policy_image]], with an optional requires expression over the options of the image's axes and the global axes that holds a policy to the profiles that run its code). The generator writes the image's own Kconfig.policies from those rows and, in wz_axes.cmake, wz_axes_policy_env: WZ_POLICY_<NAME>=<value> for each policy whose value is not upstream's, which the image's CMake adds to the cargo environment where SessionPolicy reads it. An image's Kconfig does not source the host tree's file, which names every policy: --check holds that and holds that an image that reads policies sources its own.

The rows rest on the call path from the image's own sources, traced for each of the fourteen policies, not on the crates the image links. The Zephyr admin node reads three: tx-no-progress-deadline and tx-expiry-keeps-session in every profile (its session factory builds the transmit queue from the build's policy), and declaration-sync-pacing in the fixed-memory client only (the client node of the slot profile). The other policies are read by code the image does not run (the tokio runtime, the C ABIs, the node clock and event log, the supervisor, the router) or are an assertion of the build and no run-time read. A policy the image does not name is an undefined symbol in its tree, so Zephyr stops the configuration; one it names outside its profile is Zephyr's own warning that the assignment was not honoured, which Zephyr keeps as a warning by design.
changes_bullets: deploy/wz-config.toml: three [[policy_image]] rows for zephyr-admin-node. scripts/lib/wz_config.py: the row's validation (known keys, declared policy and image, one row per pair, requires an expression over option symbols of the image's or a global axis), emit image-policies:IMAGE (the image's Kconfig.policies, shared policy text with the host file, which is unchanged byte for byte), the policy environment in emit image-cmake, the --check findings for an image that sources the host's policy file or does not source its own, and a stale own file; selftest arms for each. deploy/zephyr-admin-node: Kconfig.policies (generated), wz_axes.cmake (regenerated), Kconfig sources it, CMakeLists.txt hands wz_axes_policy_env to the cargo build. docs/build-configuration.md: a paragraph on the images' policies.
verification_bullets: wz_config.py --selftest passes (254 of 254; the preset arms skip where kconfiglib is absent) and --check passes (14 policies, 15 generated files current). The cargo line of each of the ten rows of the board table, configured with west build --cmake-only (features, whether the defaults are off, environment), is identical before and after the change with no policy stated. Configured with policies stated: the fixed-memory admin node with tx-expiry-keeps-session and tx-no-progress-deadline on is given WZ_POLICY_TX_EXPIRY_KEEPS_SESSION=on and WZ_POLICY_TX_NO_PROGRESS_DEADLINE=on; the fixed client with declaration-sync-pacing on is given WZ_POLICY_DECLARATION_SYNC_PACING=on; the fixed-memory admin peer with declaration-sync-pacing stated in a configuration file gets Zephyr's warning that it was assigned y and got n, and no environment; a policy the image does not name (subscriber-overload) stops the configuration. Round 4369.decision_summary: Two test executables replace twenty-four (wz-codecs: five files, wz-ap-demo: nineteen), and the Z8 regions scenario 7 `order3` duplicate delivery, which two consecutive fleet runs of the Z8 lane showed red, is closed at its cause: a transport events listener told of a face twice. wz-zenoh's transport and link events listeners made their watch first and then listed the open faces for the history, so a face that came up between the two was in both and the listener's callback was told of it twice. Upstream's regions test waits for three peers of a router by counting the Put events (`wait_for_n_peers`); on router 73aa9301 it counted two peers and the same peer again, stopped waiting, and began publishing while a third peer (73aa9310) was linked to the other region-3 router only. Router 73aa9300 then read itself the only gateway of that peer and carried to it a sample that the publishing peer, in the same region, had already sent it directly: one subscriber saw the sample twice and `unique_timestamps` failed. Measured on the build fleet with the test repeated: before the change 6 to 18 failures in about 400 runs (1.5 to 4.4 percent, the rate recorded before the router table phases as well, so those phases were not the cause); after it 397 of 397 pass. The earlier readings of this residue as a window between two gateways' views of a peer's links (the 4121 barrier for a dialled second link) were right that the sample was carried twice and wrong about why the scenario reached that state; the barrier stays. An accept-path barrier written for that reading was measured against the failure (9 of 414 failed, unchanged) and was not kept. Each listener now keeps a ledger of what it was told up (`FaceLedger`, wz-capi-core): a face told up is not told up again, and a down is told only for a face told up, so the order of the watch and the history does not matter.

Round 4371.decision_summary:
Three values that were fixed in the code are limits a build states. HANDSHAKE_INIT_MS and HANDSHAKE_OPEN_MS (2000 each) are the windows the INIT and OPEN phases of the unicast handshake wait for the peer's acknowledgement; SessionTimeouts::from_build() is spec_defaults() with those two, spec_defaults() stays the reference a test names, and the engines (the tokio runtime, the cooperative runtime, the lwIP and MCU session crates, the C ABIs and the Zephyr and MCU admin nodes) now hand their drive loops from_build(). The link-open, accepting and closing windows are unchanged, and the pico drop-in's connect and accept timeouts remain their own limits. A value of 0 does not compile, since a deadline of 0 fires as its phase begins.

HANDSHAKE_COOKIE_BYTES (128) is the size of the buffers in which a session on the fixed-memory profile keeps a peer's cookie (the one in the INIT acknowledgement that the node echoes in its OPEN, and the one a peer echoes that an accepting node checks). The growable profile keeps any length and does not read it. The range is a build-time check: at most 65535, the capacity the INIT body declares for its cookie, and for a node that accepts at least the widest cookie it issues itself, since below that no session it accepted could be admitted. The old comment on COOKIE_MAX called 128 the capacity the INIT and OPEN bodies declare; it was the node's own choice, the INIT body declares 65535 and the OPEN body declares none, and the comment now says so, with a test that reads the INIT body's source for the ceiling and the OPEN body's for the absence of a bound.

Round 4374.decision_summary:
The size of a query a node runs is two limits a build states: QUERY_PARAMETERS_MAX_BYTES and QUERY_ATTACHMENT_MAX_BYTES, 0 each, which is no bound and how a node behaved before them. A query from a peer whose selector parameters or attachment are longer than its bound reaches no queryable. It is counted (QueryableRegistry::oversize_refusals, saturating) and it is still a routed query, so its final is owed as for a query that matched nobody: the asker's query ends with no reply and does not wait out its timeout. The bound is read once, at the top of fire_projection, the one body that both receive paths fire a query through (the copying path and the in-place path), so the two cannot differ; a query of the node's own session is not bounded, since the caller already holds what it passed. It counts the bytes of the two fields and not the frame, and a long value is not refused for it. The codec itself states no bound on parameters (the INIT cookie's case again: what a node stores is its deployment's capacity), so the limit is the deployment's statement and not a copy of a wire number.

A limit and not a policy, because it is a number and its default is upstream's behaviour; the choice of what happens past it (run nowhere and answer with a final) is fixed, not a second switch, because a refusal that leaves the asker waiting is the one outcome no deployment wants.

This is the first of the small absent policies of the proposed order (item 3). The same round repays a clippy red in the cookie ceiling test of the previous round (a loop over one element), which that round did not run clippy on.

Round 4382.decision_summary:
The datagram-fragment-pacing policy (bool, off by default, which is upstream's behaviour of writing a message's fragments back to back) paces the fragments of one message on a UDP link. With it on, a link's writer writes at most DATAGRAM_FRAGMENT_BURST fragments in a row (default 8) and holds the next until DATAGRAM_FRAGMENT_GAP_US (default 1000, at most 1000000) has passed since the last datagram it wrote; a datagram that is not a fragment is never delayed and ends the run, and a wait that already passed is not waited again. Both limits are read only when the policy is on.

Where it sits is the decision. The first plan placed the wait in the fragment walk of the sender; reading the send path showed that walk only queues the fragments (held for the room of the link's queue, as without the policy) and that the datagrams leave at the link's writer, so the spacing is the writer's. The rule is FragmentPacer in wz-session-core: it owns no clock and takes the time as an argument, so it is tested at every value and any engine can drive it. Today the tokio engine does, in the UDP unicast writer and the multicast transmit task. QUIC datagrams (the transport paces itself) and WebSocket (a stream) are not paced. No Zephyr image, lwIP session or cooperative engine reads the policy, and since none of their image declarations names it, their trees have no symbol for it. A seal (the link closing) ends a wait at once (OutboundQueue::pause), so teardown is never held by a pace.

The same round repays a conflict between the generator and the formatter: the generator wrote a binding of a policy with a long name on one line of 101 columns and rustfmt breaks it, so wz_config.py --check and cargo fmt --check could not both pass for any policy whose name crosses the width. The generator now writes a binding past RUST_MAX_WIDTH the way the formatter leaves it, with a selftest arm for the long and the short form.

Generated: Kconfig.limits, Kconfig.policies, caps_generated.rs, policy_generated.rs, the conformance items. docs/build-configuration.md: a bullet.

Builds that must fail do, at compile time with the check's own sentence: BURST=0, GAP_US=0 and GAP_US=2000000. clippy -D warnings of wz-runtime-tokio with transport-link-udp and transport-multicast passes (its twelve warnings are in third-party ring). Round 4383.decision_summary: The third piece of the `internal` arm of Z8 is built as upstream's meaning and not as its parts: a `Runtime` is a started node that several sessions share. The crate holds its engine by an `Arc` (`RuntimeCore`: the engine, the identity, the configuration, the clocks and the shared memory a node has once), a session made on it (`session::init`) has the entities, the callbacks and the closed flag of its own, and the rule that decides whether a session is closed is one method (`SessionInner::is_closed`: its own flag, or the node closed) in place of the 32 places that asked the engine. A session that `open` makes owns its node and closes it, as before; one that `init` makes does not, and neither does the drop of its last handle: the runtime closes the node by `Runtime::close`, and the sessions on it are closed with it. The two lists of aggregated keys of upstream's `init` builder are left out because nothing here reads them, and the doc says so. The new tests found a defect in a round of mine: the ledger of round 4369 told a down only for a face it had told up, so a listener declared without history never heard of the going down of a link that was up before it (a unit test of the crate failed on it, and the crate's tests are not run by any lane). A down is told whatever the ledger holds, since only the watch tells it and it cannot be told twice; the ledger keeps its rule for an up, which is the one the duplicate delivery of scenario 7 needed.

Round 4385.decision_summary: The consumer's fourth question of round 4372 asked whether a plot should read the whole field document or a narrow door, and the measured answer was the door: a row is 67.5 times the two values a plot keeps, and most of a call writes rows a plot discards. The walk is the payload plane's own, handed the payloads it says yes to, kept between calls per selector; what it keeps is the payload and its declared encoding, read at write time by the call's declarations.

Round 4391.decision_summary:
The multicast-link-requires-iface policy (bool, off by default, which is upstream's behaviour of opening a multicast link whose locator names no interface on the first interface that can carry multicast, or on the kernel's choice when the host has none) refuses such a link. With it on, a link whose locator chose no interface is refused with an invalid-input error before any socket exists, and so is a link whose iface key this build cannot honour (a build without locator-iface resolves the key to nothing, so no interface was chosen either). Scouting sockets are not links and are not refused; a link that chose an interface opens in both arms, so what is refused is the missing choice and not every link.

Where it sits is the decision. The check is in wz-host-net on the resolved plan (Plan::require_chosen_interface), run by bind_joined for the link's receiving half and by bind_sender for its sending half, before the default interface is filled in. Checking after the fill would see an interface in every plan and refuse nothing; checking in an engine would let each engine decide again. wz-host-net has no runtime and no session-core dependency, so the policy reaches it as a field of SocketConfig (link_requires_iface, false = upstream), and the tokio engine fills that field in McastSocketConfig::neutral(), the one conversion to SocketConfig, from SessionPolicy::from_build(). Only the tokio engine reads the policy: no Zephyr image, lwIP session or cooperative engine does, and none of their image declarations names it, so their trees have no symbol for it.

Round 4392.decision_summary:
A ledger round can now travel in a commit as a descriptor, and one script files it however it arrives. This is the first step of moving the push queue from land.sh's clone-local lock to the bx landing queue, whose integrator cherry-picks a commit onto the remote tip and runs the repository's declared actions: it has no lock, no file outside the commit and no way to say a round number, so the round has to be data in the commit and its number has to be taken on the tree it lands on.

The descriptor (docs/rounds/pending/<slug>.toml, form stated in scripts/lib/round_descriptor.py) holds the impact ids and the four prose fields and no number, because the number is the one fact a commit cannot know: it is the store's last round plus one at the moment of landing. scripts/file-round.sh reads the store's last round, files each pending descriptor as the next round through append-round.sh, and deletes it; a tree with no descriptor is left unchanged. The number is a function of the tree it runs on, which is what lets an integrator run it again on a rebased candidate and get the number right for the new base. Nothing outside the tree enters the filing.

Two choices are the decision. First, the filing is a bx action (file-round) declared in bx.toml and not a hook or a step of the integrator, so it is the repository's own, runs on a copy on a build machine, and is judged against its declared outputs before anything is written. Second, land.sh files descriptors through the same script, so there is one way to file a round and the old path (ledger arguments after the double dash) is the same append underneath; land.sh refuses a batch that has both, since that would file two rounds. The read of the last round is written once (scripts/lib/ledger-round.sh) and both callers source it, so the two cannot number differently. The decisions this follows are recorded outside the repository: acknowledgement as a committed row, a numberless derived subject, the push gate replaced by an integrator check, the confidential-vocabulary gate run on queue refs, and the permission wording, which is the owner's to change.

The acknowledgement still travels as WZ_ACK_RED on the pushing process and has to become a row in the pushed range that names a run and no round number. Gate 0p (lock and token) still refuses any push to main that is not land.sh's, so an integrator's push would be refused until the gate recognises it. Round 4393.decision_summary:
Acknowledging a red hosted run is now a row of docs/hosted-red-acks.md that the range being pushed adds, and the environment variable that used to carry it (WZ_ACK_RED, with land.sh --ack-red) is gone. This is the second step of moving the push queue to the bx landing queue, and the reason is a principle and not a convenience: a verdict has to be a function of the commit and the tree it lands on. A queue integrator cherry-picks a commit onto the remote tip, runs the repository's pre-push hook on the result with the push's own stdin line, and pushes for the author; the author's environment is not there, so a gate that reads it gives the integrator a different verdict than it gave the author. The row is in the commit, so whatever runs the hook over the commit reaches the same verdict.

The row keeps the three properties the variable had, because they are what made the acknowledgement an act of reading and not a formality. It is per push: only a row ADDED in the pushed range counts, so a row of an earlier push cannot cover a later red silently (the file's own history repeats rows for one run because the variable was per invocation, and the rule stays). It is per run: the id is matched whole between backticks in the run cell, so one run's digits never acknowledge another. It is by the author: the first column is the author's own label and the gate does not read it, which removes the round number from the acknowledgement, and with it the --round precondition of land.sh (the text of a row named the round, so the round had to be known before filing; a commit holds no such number, since the descriptor round's number is taken on the tree it lands on).

Where the check lives is the decision. The reading of a range for rows is one small tool with a selftest (scripts/lib/hosted_red_ack.py), the previous-run gate takes the range as a third argument and calls it, and the pre-push hook passes the range it already computed for its other gates. Keeping the variable as a second accepted form was refused: two ways to acknowledge is the same unreproducible verdict with a door left open for it.

Round 4399.decision_summary:
The pre-push hook now reads what each ref of a push IS before it grades it, and gate 0p lets a clone marked as the queue integrator's push to main. This is the third step of moving the push queue to the bx landing queue. Until now the hook read one kind of push, a branch, with the last ref of the push as its range. An integrator's push is one atomic transaction that carries several kinds at once (the branch, the queue's log, the deletion of the item refs it has finished), and reading the last ref there grades the log's chain as though it were the branch. A submitted item and the log are also published to the public origin before anything lands, so what makes a publication irreversible has to apply to them.

Each ref is classified (scripts/lib/push-refs.sh): main, a queue item, the queue's log or lease, or another ref. A queue ref gets the three public gates and nothing else, over exactly what it adds: the confidential vocabulary, a line naming a home directory, an identity that must not be public. The repository's own gates (schema pin, SSOT, tests) are not run on it, because an item is judged by the integrator on the tip it will land on and the log is no repository content. A ref whose range cannot be bounded is refused, since an ungraded public push is what these gates exist to stop. An unknown name in the queue's namespace is graded as a record, the strictest reading. A push of only queue refs ends after those gates; a push that also carries the branch continues with the branch's range, which no longer includes the queue refs.

A chain that is new, or whose old value this clone does not hold, has no base to subtract, and a bare tip is no range: git diff of a bare tip compares with the working tree, which graded a log chain against the checkout and blocked it for text it did not contain. Such a chain is graded from an empty base commit (fixed identity and dates, so the same object everywhere, reachable from no ref), which makes "everything the chain holds" an ordinary base..tip range for all three gates.

Gate 0p accepts a push to main when the clone's configuration says it is the integrator's (wz.land-integrator, a boolean the owner sets where the service runs); otherwise the lock and token logic is unchanged. The marker is a clone fact and not part of any item, so it does not make a verdict depend on the item's author; it is spoofable, and the real wall is the server's ruleset, to be enabled after a week of the queue without it.

Round 4400.decision_summary: The readers' loss under a busy writer of the snapshot tables, left unseparated by round 4388, is separated (docs/router-table-snapshots.md, section 6.7). The Puts a second and the time a reader ran a core both moved with the load of the shared hosts by more than the effect, so the reading is the readers' instructions and cycles a Put under perf, one window kind to a process. Loading versions is not the cost: at the declaring writer's rate a version that changes nothing costs the readers nothing a run tells. The writer's own work on the host is at most half of it (5.7 % more cycles from a writer declaring twice as often into a router nobody reads). The rest, 2.3 % more instructions and some 5 % more cycles, is what the readers do because the tables changed, and a profile names three parts: readers freed the retired versions' path copies, the route caches moved their inputs at every version, and a reader behind the cache computed routes it could not keep. The first contradicted read-copy-update, whose readers never reclaim: the cell now keeps replaced versions by their count and the writer frees those no reader holds at its next publish and at each grace period; the readers' profile no longer has the frees and the writer's has them. The gain in Puts a second was not told apart from the hosts' load and is not claimed. Round 4388 added two ungated tests to `router_forward` without moving Layer C1AY's counts; they move here with this round's pair test, each arm's count as its command printed it.

Round 4401.decision_summary:
Every product this checkout's lanes and oracle scripts write -- cargo target directories, CMake build directories, installed oracles, logs, Python bytecode -- can now be placed outside the checkout by one variable, WZ_ARTIFACT_ROOT, and with it set nothing is written into the checkout. A consumer mounts this checkout read-only (its files are shared between worktrees as hard links) and could only run the upstream lanes by making their run directory writable; the root removes that exception. Unset, every path is where it always was.

The rule is one: a product of the tree path <rel> is at <checkout>/<rel> unset and at $WZ_ARTIFACT_ROOT/<rel> set, the layout mirroring the tree. It is stated once in scripts/lib/artifact-root.sh and read three ways, the shell resolver (wz_artifact_root_init, $WZ_ARTIFACTS, wz_artifact_dir), scripts/lib/artifact_root.py and wz_codegen_build::artifact / artifact_dir, each taking the variable as given and the checkout from its own place; no reader re-derives it. Mirroring was chosen over a table of names so that every path a lane, a test or a comment already names keeps naming the same product, and only the prefix moves.

The cargo calls (over a thousand in run-ci.sh, more in other scripts and in tests that spawn cargo) are not edited. Under a root a cargo shim first on PATH gives each cargo workspace of the checkout its mirrored target directory, honours a target directory the caller chose, and refuses one inside the checkout, so a write that would land there fails at once with the path named instead of landing. A program on PATH reaches cargo however it is called, which a shell function does not.

Whether a lane writes nothing into the checkout is measured, not only read: Layer Ero mounts the checkout and every target link out of it read-only (a bwrap user namespace, or sudo's mount namespace on a hosted runner), builds the pico oracle and runs Layer Ewire with WZ_PICO_REQUIRE=1 and the root as the only writable place. artifact_root_lint.py reads every tracked script, gate and crate for a product path spelled past the root, with line-scoped exemptions that must still excuse something.

The first Ero run found a write that was not a spelling: zenoh-pico's CMakeLists configure_file writes include/zenoh-pico.h into its SOURCE directory, so every pico build wrote into the vendor submodule, with or without a root. zenoh-pico-sys now configures from a copy of the source staged in its OUT_DIR, and its build cache is discarded when it was made from another source directory. The upstream CMake is unchanged; the fix is where wz drives it.

Round 4403.decision_summary: The atomic store stops growing as one file. Measured before: 56 MB, past GitHub's 50 MB advisory, about 2.4 MB a week, and 48 percent of it the publishable half of each entry written again although only 22 of 4389 entries differ. The owner chose both remedies (2026-11-08). Mnemosyne ee934276 (its Round 1344, schema 49) writes a publishable field only where it differs from its audit twin, and lets a store seal its frozen ledger into segment files the main file pins by sha256. This store is sealed in segments of 500: the main file is 3.8 MB and holds sections, inventory and the open tail; eight segments hold the rest, 29 MB in all, and a round rewrites only the main file. Scripts that read the ledger read it through atomic_ledger.py, which joins the segments and refuses one whose bytes are not the pinned ones; the push runs its check. Round 4410.decision_summary:
The policy entity-link-restriction (bool, off by default, which is upstream's behaviour of letting every entity use every link of the session) is added, with its mechanism in the tokio registry. An entity can be limited to a set of links: a publish and a query go out only on the named links, and a subscriber and a queryable are declared, and replayed to a link that comes up later, only to the named links, so they hear and answer nothing that arrives over the others. This generalises locality, which says whether an entity takes part in this session's traffic, other nodes', or both, to the second question a node with several links has, which ones.

The value is a type of the session core and not a field of one engine: LinkRestriction is Any or a non-empty set of slots below 64, held in one machine word, so it costs an entity eight bytes and no allocation and an engine with one link per node can read it where it reads locality. A link is named by a slot the engine derives from how the link came to be. In the tokio registry the dialling role is slot 0 and the listener bound nth is slot n + 1, so the faces a listener accepts share its slot and a set that names it names all of them, the later ones included; a face the numbering cannot place has no slot and a limited entity does not use it, because an unnamed link cannot have been named. An empty set is refused where it is built, since an entity that may use no link is unreachable and not restricted.

Three placements are the decision. The check is made where the registry already fans out (the one fan-out every publish shares, the one query fan, the declaration walk, and the replay onto a new face), so no site decides it for itself and a face that joins later means the same as one that was there. Declaring to the named links only is also what limits what an entity hears, because each face holds its own copy of every entity, so the receive side needed no second check. The local plane is not a link and is always reached, and a multicast group has no slot, so a limited entity is not put on one. The policy's whole effect is a refusal at the entry point (LinkRestriction::admit_in_build): with it off, a call that states a set is refused and says why instead of being ignored, so a build without the policy has upstream's entities only. The registry itself does not read the policy, as the multicast refusal's plan does not, so a test names either arm without a second binary.

carry_forward_bullets: Open: the mechanism is not reachable from any API yet. The Rust API builders (publisher, put, subscriber, queryable, get, querier) and the C ABI do not state a set, so LinkRestriction::admit_in_build has no caller; the next step plumbs a set through them and refuses it when the policy is off. Only the tokio peer and client registry reads the set: the router engine, the cooperative engine and the lwIP session do not, and an entity in them is unrestricted. Liveliness tokens and liveliness subscribers have no locality or link set at all and are not covered. The policy-on arm was not built as a whole image: the registry honours a set whatever the policy, and the policy's own effect is the refusal, tested with an explicit flag. A physical link under one multilink face has no slot, so a set cannot name one of several links of a face. The numbering gives the dialling role one slot, so a session that dials several endpoints does not distinguish them. Round 4411.decision_summary:
bx.toml declares the landing queue ([land], bx RFC 0024), the fourth step of moving the push queue to bx. The values are chosen, not defaulted, and each says what the repository wants of the queue. The judge is the repository's own pre-push hook (no checks bundle), run for the landing push's own line, so what the queue accepts is exactly what a push would have been given, and the hook that grades each ref by what it holds (step three) is the one gate rather than a second one beside it. The ledger round is derived: the file-round action files it on the candidate with the number the store gives it there, and the derived commit has a fixed message that states no number, because the store is the one place that knows it. regen-codegen is not derived, since land.sh never regenerated either and each candidate would pay a whole regeneration. The window is 1 (no speculation): the hook is heavy, the cores are shared, and a window above 1 runs several hook runs at once; it is raised when the queue has measured a wait that speculation would remove. The rebase strategy and the remote and branch are the defaults, written out so the declaration says them.

Nothing is switched on by this. No integrator runs for this repository: the lease of the queue is held by none and the queue is empty, and scripts/land.sh stays the way main is pushed until an integrator has landed a week of rounds. A clone marked wz.land-integrator lifts gate 0p's lock requirement for every push it makes, so only the integrator's own clone is marked.

Round 4419.decision_summary:
The link set of entity-link-restriction is reachable from the Rust API: the builders of a publisher (and the put and delete it makes), a subscriber, a queryable, a get and a querier take .allowed_links(..), beside allowed_origin and allowed_destination. The set is stored in the builder, threaded into the engine-facing declaration of each entity and passed to the registry doors that already honour it, and a set that is stated is refused at the point the builder resolves when the build's policy is off, with the policy's own sentence. A set that is not stated takes exactly the path it took before.

The door is behind a new non-default crate feature, link-restriction, and the re-export of the types with it. This is the decision that was not obvious: the repository's public-surface gate refuses any public item the crate has and upstream does not, a wz-only door belongs in the namespace for wz extensions, and until that namespace exists the door is kept out of the default surface by a feature, so a user who wants it asks for it and nobody else sees a changed surface. The plumbing, the policy check and the tests of the default build are not behind the feature.

Two placements are worth stating. A declared publisher or querier carries its set and each put or get made through it is checked again, with the same result, so a handle cannot outlive the policy's refusal. The router engine, which holds the declarations of every face it serves and has no per-entity link of its own, refuses a set with its own sentence rather than ignoring it.

Round 4420.decision_summary:
The policy targeted-query (bool, off by default, which is upstream's behaviour of sending a query to every link whose peers declared a matching queryable) is added with its mechanism in the tokio registry. A query can be addressed to one node by the identity its link's handshake gave it, and then goes out on that node's link only. This is the second question about where a query goes, beside the link set of entity-link-restriction, and it shares its place: the registry already fans a query out per face and each face already carries the identity of its node, so the check is one comparison in the loop that exists.

The target names a node and not a link or a queryable, because a node is what a caller knows and the link that reaches it is the engine's business. A node with no link leaves no leg and the query is not widened to the others: widening would answer a question the caller did not ask, from nodes it meant to leave out, so a query for an absent node ends with no replies and says so by having none. The session-local leg and a multicast group are left out of an addressed query, since neither is that node's link. A session keeps one face per node, so the match is at most one leg. When a link set is stated as well, the node's link has to be in the set.

The fan-out took a locality and then a link set and now would take a third argument, so the reach of a get is one value (QueryReach: the set and the target) and the options struct states it. The value's rules and the refusal a build without the policy gives live in the session core (peer_target), the registry reads no policy, and the entry point refuses a target when the policy is off, as the link set does.

Round 4423.decision_summary:
The policy publisher-admission-retry (bool, off by default, which is upstream's behaviour of waiting for room and, when a droppable message meets a congested lane, counting a drop and returning success) lets one publish state a bounded retry: some attempts with a delay between them, used only when no face accepted the frame. Upstream's call cannot tell a queued frame from a congestion drop, and a caller that must know has nothing to react to; the retry makes the no-room outcome a thing the fan-out can see and act on.

The probe is the decision. The send path already had a no-wait question (it returns the message back when the lane has no room, counts nothing and closes nothing), used by the router egress; the publish now has a probing form built on it, and the fan-out classifies each face as queued, no room, skipped or refused. If any face took the frame nothing is retried, and the faces with no room are skipped as a congestion drop skips them today, so a frame is never offered twice to a face that took it. If none did and some had no room, the fan-out waits the delay and offers the frame again to those faces only, up to the attempts, then ends with nothing delivered; it does not close the session and it does not count a drop. A payload that must be fragmented can never be sent without waiting, so a probe of it is sent the waiting way and is never retried, which keeps what a publish did before.

The pure pass loop is separate from the faces, so its rules (a taker ends it, only no-room faces are re-offered, the waits total attempts times the delay) are tested without a full lane, which no registry test can build. The wait is a blocking sleep on the caller's thread, as a blocking send already is, because the registry's clock sleeps only as a future. The policy is read by the entry point (admit_in_build refuses a stated retry when it is off) and not by the fan-out, as the other per-entity policies are. Shared-memory publishes and the plain-put lane keep their old paths, the lane because it waits and knows no retry, so a publish that states a retry is taken off it.

Round 4424.decision_summary:
The policy reliable-gap-reconnect (a choice: off, until-declarations-synced, always; off by default, which is upstream's behaviour of accepting a forward jump of the reliable sequence number and dropping one that does not advance) lets a build end the link when a reliable frame shows that frames were lost. With a reacting mode the frame that shows the gap is dropped and the link is reported lost, so the existing supervisor reopens the session and redoes the declaration sync, which is the only way to get back frames the reliable channel promised and did not deliver. Best-effort channels are untouched, since loss there is not a fault.

The judge is widened and not replaced: the sequence-number admit returned a bool, so a gap was invisible, and it now has a judged form (accept, a gap with the count missing, stale) with the bool form as a thin wrapper, so every existing caller and test is unchanged. The reaction sits where the driver loop already ends a link for a protocol fault, beside the unknown-priority precedent, as a new lost cause, so nothing about reconnection is new: a lost link already rides the supervisor. With the policy off the code takes the old bool path unchanged.

until-declarations-synced reacts only while the peer's initial declarations have not all arrived, because a gap during the replay of declarations is repaired by the reconnect that replays them again, and after that a gap would be a loss the reconnect cannot make good. The peer's final was readable only in the tokio session, after the sequence gate, so it is mirrored into an atomic on the session core, set when a final of the initial interest arrives and cleared when the session is reopened; a final that answers an interest the node itself sent is not the peer's. The pure decision (mode and that flag) is one const function with its truth table tested.

A command that scripts/lib/read-only-tree.sh runs in a read-only checkout now sees the caller's whole environment, with WZ_ARTIFACT_ROOT on top, on both of its branches. Before, the bwrap branch (a build machine) passed the environment through, while the sudo branch (a hosted runner) passed what `sudo -E` left plus a chosen list of PATH, HOME and LD_LIBRARY_PATH. So a lane saw different variables depending on which branch its host took, and the difference showed up only on hosted runs. Measured on a fleet host by forcing the sudo branch: the command ran as the caller's uid but saw USER=root and LOGNAME=root, lost PERL5LIB, PYTHONPATH and LD_PRELOAD, and gained SUDO_* and a changed TERM. USER=root matters to a test that re-runs itself in a namespace, because NetnsPair::test_inside hands USER to runuser.

Round 4373 fixed it in NetnsPair::test_inside by carrying the whole environment. 79ce50c9b9 fixed this script by adding LD_LIBRARY_PATH to its list. A list can only name the variables someone has already lost, so the sudo branch now does what the Rust twin does. The caller's environment is read NUL-separated, passed across as arguments, and restored with `env -i` after setpriv drops back to the caller's uid. `-E` is no longer needed, because nothing is taken from sudo's environment.

Round 4432.decision_summary:
The policy multi-route-atomic-tx (bool, off by default, which is upstream's behaviour of sending a put to each link on its own terms) lets one publish ask to reach all of the links it uses or none. Upstream sends the frame to every link and each link whose queue is full drops it or waits for room by itself, so one put can reach some links and not others, and a caller that treats the links as one route cannot use that.

Asking each link whether it has room and then sending is not atomic, since another sender can fill a lane between the question and the send. So the decision is a two-phase reservation on the link's outbound queue. The queue already had a promise primitive (a permit that counts as occupied room until it is used or dropped, which a waiting sender and a sender that already has room never share); the link seam now exposes it as BoxedLinkDriver::try_reserve_room, a provided method whose default grants a trivial permit for a driver with no queue, with a RoomPermit that is owned, Send and gives its room back when dropped. Every driver over the queue and both swap seams forward it; a wrapper that did not would promise room that nothing holds. The session asks it for the lane a message would leave on and sends under it through a dispatch stage that skips the ask for room, because the ask would count the sender's own promise against the lane.

The permit is held across the send and dropped after it, and is not converted into the frame inside the enqueue. The queue's enqueue never consults the bound (only the ask does), so holding the permit through the send can only make the lane read fuller than it is for that interval and never emptier, which is the conservative side of the atomicity; converting inside the enqueue would have meant threading the permit through every enqueue path (heap, pooled, lent, inline, batch). A reserved send waits for its conduit's lock where a probe gives up, because a promise that failed on a lock would break the atomicity; the lock is held across a wait for room only by a sender whose own wait ends at its deadline and who cannot be given the promised room.

The registry runs phase one over the faces the publish may use, in order, and stops at the first face with no room: every reservation taken is dropped, nothing is sent to any face, group or subscriber of the session, no sequence number is spent, and the publish ends with a delivery count of zero without closing the session. Otherwise phase two sends to each face that promised room under its own reservation, and the multicast groups and the session's own subscribers are delivered to after it. A face that is down, or was never told an alias, answers absent before it is asked for room and takes no part. A publish that also states an admission retry reserves again after the delay, once the aborted pass gave its room back. The pure two-phase loop is separate from the faces, as the retry's pass loop is, so its rules are tested without a full lane.

Round 4433.decision_summary:
The two policies that were reachable only from the registry are reachable from the Rust API, each behind a non-default crate feature, as the link set of entity-link-restriction is. A get and a querier take .target_peer(zid) with the node's ZenohId behind targeted-query, and a publisher and the put and delete a session makes take .admission_retry(retry) with an AdmissionRetry behind admission-retry. The value is stored in the builder, carried by the declared publisher or querier, threaded through the session's publish and query path into the engine-facing request, and set on the options struct the registry already reads (QueryOptions::with_target_peer, PublishOptions::with_admission_retry). The registry side needed nothing: the query reach and the publish fan-out already read both fields, so only the front half was missing.

A value that is stated is refused at the point the builder resolves when the build's policy is off, with the policy's own sentence, by calling the policy's admit_in_build; a value that is not stated takes exactly the path it took before. The refusal comes at the declaration of a publisher or a querier and again at each put or get made through it, so a handle cannot outlive the refusal. The router engine reads neither value and refuses a stated one with its own sentence rather than widening a query or dropping a retry without saying so.

The decision that was not obvious is the shape of the stored values. The node is held as the ZenohId the crate already spells identities with and becomes the identity bytes only where the tokio engine converts it, so the field exists in every build; the retry is the policy value itself in a build with an engine and an empty type in one without, as the link set is. Both features are kept out of the default surface for the reason link-restriction is: the public-surface gate refuses an item upstream lacks.

Round 4434.decision_summary:
The all-or-none publish of multi-route-atomic-tx, which was reachable only from the registry, is reachable from the Rust API behind a non-default crate feature, atomic-publish, as the link set and the retry are behind theirs. A publisher and the put and delete a session makes take .all_links_or_none(). The method takes no argument: the form is only ever stated, never stated as false, so an unstated publish keeps exactly the path it had. The value is a bool stored in the builder, carried by the declared publisher, threaded through the session's publish path into the engine-facing request, and set on the options struct the registry already reads (PublishOptions::with_atomic_tx). The registry side needed nothing: the two-phase reservation already reads the field, so only the front half was missing.

A statement is refused at the point the builder resolves when the build's policy is off, with the policy's own sentence, by calling atomic_tx::admit_in_build. The refusal comes at the declaration of a publisher and again at each put or delete made through it, so a handle cannot outlive the refusal. The router engine reads no reservation and refuses a stated publish with its own sentence, at declaration and at use, rather than sending it to each face on its own terms without saying so. A publish that states both a retry and all-or-none hands both to the engine, which reserves again after the delay.

The decision that was not obvious is the value type. The retry is an empty type in a build without an engine because it carries numbers that only an engine reads; all-or-none carries none, so a plain bool is the same value in every build and needs no second definition, and the admit function of a build without an engine accepts it because the feature that states it implies the engine.

Round 4438.decision_summary:
The four default-off statements the session model and the tokio registry already read (the links an entity may use, a query addressed to one node, a retry for a publish no link had room for, an all-or-none publish) are statable from the zenoh-c C ABI, behind a new non-default feature of crates/wz-capi-c, switch-doors, which is a capability like lifecycle-doors: declared in deploy/wz-config.toml, off by default, implying query and queryable, and forwarded to the core by name.

Nothing is a field of a z_ option struct and nothing is a new z_, zc_ or ze_ export: those layouts are upstream's, held to the installed header by the footprint gate, and those symbols are held to the reference library's by the symbol census. The surface is wz_capi_c_ symbols declared in the wz header: three transparent structs (an entity statement of a link mask; a publish statement of a link mask, attempts, delay and an all-or-none flag; a query statement of a link mask and a target identity), a default function for each that writes the statement of nothing, and seven doors, wz_capi_c_put_ext, wz_capi_c_delete_ext, wz_capi_c_declare_publisher_ext, wz_capi_c_get_ext, wz_capi_c_declare_querier_ext, wz_capi_c_declare_subscriber_ext and wz_capi_c_declare_queryable_ext. Each door takes what its z_ twin takes and one more argument, a pointer to a statement, null for none.

The z_ functions are thin wrappers over the same bodies, which now take the statement as an argument: the z_ function passes the statement that states nothing, applying it changes no option, and so a call that states nothing is the call it was, in every build and whatever the policy. The carriers of a statement (crates/wz-capi-c/src/statement.rs) are not behind the feature, so the shared bodies compile without it; the doors and the structs are.

A stated value is passed through the matching admit_in_build (LinkRestriction, admission_retry, atomic_tx, peer_target) before anything is sent or declared. With the policy off the door answers a new result code, WZ_CAPI_C_E_POLICY_OFF (-102), outside zenoh-c's range as the two wz codes before it are; a declaration leaves its out-parameter in the gravestone state; a closure, a payload and the owned fields of the options are consumed on a refusal as on a success, which is what the z_ twins do on every path. Not Z_EINVAL, because the same call is right in a build whose policy is on. What no engine can hold is Z_EINVAL whatever the policy: a retry of no pass or no delay, more than 255 passes or 65535 milliseconds, a target that is the zero identity. The policy answers before the numbers for a retry that is built as stated (zero attempts beside a delay), as the model's own admit does.

A session that is a node reads none of the four: its data plane writes to its faces by its own tables. A call that states one there answers Z_EUNAVAILABLE, the code every operation a node does not carry already answers, and sends or declares nothing; a call that states nothing is carried as before. A subscriber and a queryable declared with links go through declare_subscriber_on_links and declare_queryable_on_links; the plain declarations were already those calls with no restriction and the literal wire key, so the shared bodies call the links form for both.

A target is the 16 bytes of the z_id_t with its trailing zero bytes cut, which is how the engine names a node and how a face records it, as the Rust API's peer_bytes does. A publisher folds its statement into the options every put and delete on it starts from, at the declaration; the plain-put lane already answers none for a stated retry, all-or-none or restricted links, so no put reaches it past the statement.

The ABI revision of the wz door set moves from 11 to 12 (ten new symbols and the code), and the symbol pin lists them as the build the lane runs, which has the feature on, as it has the others.

Round 4442.decision_summary:
A consumer that lists a live capture's rows asked for the field document's rows after its cursor at every step and could not keep up at 20,000 small messages a second: a row was about 3.7 KB and about 17 us to write, and its own parse cost as much again. Its list reads what each row says about the message (carried, payload_decode, above_transport, sn, chain, first_byte, l2, the coordinates) and none of the row's field tree, which it asks for one picked message at a time. It asked for those facts in binary, the shape to be chosen here.

Measured first, on a capture of 64-byte pushes (benches/row_facts_cost.rs, 20,004 rows): with the trees a row was 3,756 bytes and 14.8 us; without them 970 bytes and 4.4 us. The trees are 74% of a row's bytes and 70% of the call. So the cost is the trees, and the facts are already computed by one writer from one walk.

The rows without their trees are written by that same writer: fields_json::Trees::Left leaves out a row's fields tree and a completed chain's above_transport.fields trees and nothing else, from the same walk. A second writer of the same facts in a binary layout was refused: every fact would have two derivations, held to each other by hope. The document is its own, row_facts revision 1, as this library already names a shape by a document (the selection documents were split off the field document for the same reason); its key set is the field document's at revision 60 less the two keys only a tree writes (a node's kind and selector_path), its families the same less kind, and its carries the same with the fields a row's offset_space and a chain's carried_state brought taken out. A test holds the set to the field document's newest, so a key added to a row cannot reach row_facts under a stale revision.

The binary form is RFC 8949's mapping of that JSON onto CBOR (cbor_of_json), key for key, definite lengths and preferred serialization, so the binary rows are the one writer's rows and a reader that knows the field document knows this one. The conversion costs 1.9 us a row over the treeless text (707 bytes a row against 970); a native CBOR writer would save that, and it is a carry, not done here, because it is a second writer of every key the document has.

The door is wz_dissect_live_row_facts_since and wz_dissect_live_row_facts_take, ABI 55. Bytes are not a string and this ABI does not allocate what it hands back, so they go into a buffer the caller owns: when it holds them the call is over, and when it does not the handle keeps the document until the take copies it out, because asking again would move the handle's memory a second time. The memory rule does not move. The handle keeps a FieldsMemory per shape, so a consumer that steps with this door and asks the field door for one picked row leaves each walk where it was; the memory document's fields group counts both.

The field document moves to revision 60: a datagram flow's disagreements group (count, named, and each named frame's at) has been written since the field layer's first round and no key set listed it. Found when row_facts was held to its key set; the pin population gains a document that names a disagreement.

Round 4447.decision_summary: The capture crate did not build with its field walker and without its default features (`--no-default-features --features dissect`): seven uses of the selector's row judgement, which is defined only with the network codecs, and three matches on the carried unit that left out its fragment arms. The second error was the first clue. `dissect` selects the session core's own `dissect`, which turns on the push, request, response and declare codecs, and the session core's transport writers, which turn on its reassembly. The capture crate reads its own two features, `network-codecs` and `reassembly`, to know what the decoder below it can do, so this build had a decoder that read every network message and fragment and a crate that said it could not. Gating the judgement, the selector doors and the items only they read made the library and its tests compile, and then the test written for a build without the codecs failed: a Push such a build "cannot name" was decoded and counted. That is the contradiction itself, and no gating removes it. So `dissect` now names the two features it was already turning on underneath, and the gating was not kept. Every consumer of `dissect` (the dissection C library, the analyzer and the fuzz targets) already had both through the crate's defaults, so no build that compiled before changes; the build without the default features at all, where the no-codec test belongs, still has neither.

Round 4448.decision_summary: The row-facts door hands its rows as the CBOR form of the treeless field document, and that conversion read the JSON text twice: once to count every container's members and once to write with those counts, because a definite-length head is written before the members it counts. The counting pass cost nearly as much as the writing one. The second writer that would avoid the conversion altogether was not built, for the reason the converter's module states: it would be a second derivation of every fact on a row. Instead the converter now reads the text once. A container's head is written as one byte when it opens, which is the whole head of any container of fewer than 24 members, and completed when it closes; a container of 24 members or more has its argument bytes put in after that byte there, the members written since moving once. The output is the same bytes: preferred serialization and definite lengths, as before. The head of a given width is now written by one function, which both the open writer and the close use.

That keeps the submodule only read, and moves no modification time, which the incremental build relies on. The artifact-root helper names this consumption shape as supported, so the script is held to it.
